maintopic: RECROSSING OP 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: RECROSSING OP 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
Yesterday I directed a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In his absence, it was answered by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). It is found on page 253 of Hansard and reads as follows:
Were members of the United Nations consulted about the reported recrossing of the 38th parallel by United Nations troops? If so, did Canada express an opinion, and what was it?
The Prime Minister answered, and I asked a supplementary question to which I am most anxious to secure an answer. It reads:
Has Canada made any representations to the secretary general or to the United Nations concerning reconsideration of the implied permission which was granted to the troops last October?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secreiary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RECROSSING OP 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has directed my attention to these questions and has asked me to reply to them, which I am glad to do.
There is some doubt as to the exact details about the reported crossing of the 38th parallel by a South Korean detachment. Apparently it was a purely tactical movement and on a small scale, and does not indicate that any decision has been taken for a major crossing of the line, even if military conditions make that possible.
In reply to the second question, Mr. Speaker, Canada has not made any representations to the secretary general or to the United Nations concerning the question of the recrossing of the 38th parallel by United Nations forces. However, representatives of governments with forces participating in Korean operations have had informal discussions recently with the United States representatives in regard to this and other matters arising out of the Korean campaign. These discussions have included a Canadian representative. As a result of these discussions, I think I can state that the political significance of any new move across the parallel deep into North Korean territory is fully appreciated. At this moment I would not like to add anything to this observation beyond repeating my view that any decision taken in this matter should be a collective
[Mr. Claxton.l
one, including particularly those governments who are participating in United Nations-Korean operations, of which the most important is the United States of America.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, February 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. FEBRUARY 13, 1951
The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith
W. H. McMillan for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Herridge.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. McMillan) and the seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I join with the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) in his expression of the opinion they were good Liberal addresses. This afternoon it is my intention to make a good Liberal address. Everyone may not agree that it will be a good Liberal address. However, I can assure you it will not be a Social Credit address, nor will it be a C.C.F. address, nor a Tory address; therefore, it will be a Liberal address, good or bad.
I am going to deal first, Mr. Speaker, with controls. I should have liked to deal with the previous C.C.F. subamendment. In my opinion it was a Red subamendment, but since it has been discarded I suppose I am not at liberty to deal with it. However, this control subamendment which is now before the house is a better one. Of course, that is the way the C.C.F. generally operates. I know about the C.C.F. party because I was brought up among them- in Saskatchewan. They wave a flag, and if the people will follow it, fine and dandy; if not, then they drop that flag and pick up another one and wave it. In my opinion they have a flag this time which more people will follow. Already it appears as though they have support for this subamendment from the other two opposition groups. I believe the amendment calls upon members of parliament for a vote of nonconfidence in the government for not imposing controls.
I represent, sir, a constituency composed of farmers and many labouring men in and around the Estevan area. I have had many little cards sent to me, as have most of the members of this house. On checking these cards I find that the ones I have received, and I have hundreds of them, came from the labour group in my constituency. This card says that controls should be applied immediately to protect the living standards of our families. I am not opposed to controls, Mr. Speaker, in principle. I am going to answer, through the record, the people of my constituency who sent me these cards, because I have far too many to answer personally. I am going to say to them that in my opinion a large majority are sincere in asking for controls. They ask me for my support. Had they also requested control of wages, I assure them
that they would have obtained my support. However, I have neither read nor heard anything from union leaders suggesting that wages should be controlled. I would say, therefore, that at the moment they are barking up the wrong tree. They should ask their union leaders to come out and say they are willing to accept controls across the board.
I am going to deal with the farmers in a moment, but on this same card it says that rent controls should be maintained, and it urges me to support this legislation. As to rent control, again I say that in principle I am not opposed to it. But I think rent control is a provincial responsibility. I definitely think that the matter should be handled provincially, because it could be handled more efficiently in that way than by the federal government. For instance, I do not think anyone would suggest that the premier of his province and his government and the city councils could not sit down and work out a rent control scheme for that province better than could the federal government.
I will now speak for a moment about the farmers in my constituency, and I think what I say about them is applicable to the farmers in many parts of Canada. I have not read or heard anything to the effect that the farmers have said they want to be controlled across the board. I do not think farmers on the whole are opposed to controls; but at the moment I cannot see what a farmer has to gain by being controlled. The things that he has to sell, with the exception of beef, in recent months have gone down in price, and the things that he has to buy have gone up. I cannot see where he would benefit from controls at the moment. However, if the farmers want to come out, through their leaders and through the farmers' union, of which I am a member, and say that they want controls across the board, they will definitely get my support. At the moment, however, they have not said so, and I do not think the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has said so either.
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in the special session last fall, said that in his opinion one of the reasons why the government was not putting on controls, was that the people of Canada were not yet ready for them. I am quite satisfied that the farmers and labour in my constituency have not definitely stated that they want controls. I join to some extent with the official opposition, speaking through their leader, who intimated in the first part of his speech that he was in favour of controls and then before he finished said that we should support the C.C.F. amendment just on principle, even if

The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith we did not agree with it. At one time he is in favour of controls, and at another time he is not in favour of controls. I join with him and take the same position, because I do not know whether that would help the situation.
Some good comments have been made with regard to the speech from the throne. The opposition has given the house some food for thought. However, I have been less impressed by the criticism this time than I was in previous sessions when I was a new member, and, I admit, one who was very green and still is. They are now criticizing the government for not doing anything to head off inflation. When I came here first I sat in this chair and heard the members of the opposition say that prior to the session the government had hidden a depression. They said that we had a depression in Canada and that for election reasons the government had kept it out of sight; that we had lost our markets and that prices were going down. Representing the constituency which I have the honour to represent, Mr. Speaker, I sat in my chair and shivered. I thought that possibly what they were saying was true. However, it did not turn out to be the case. It is well to recall that the predictions which the opposition make do not seem to turn out; I do not know why.
Last spring, when it was said that we had an unemployment situation in Canada, the official opposition-and I think the other two oppositions joined with them-again called upon this government to bring in a public works program, or to start a building program across this country, so that it would take care of this unemployment and head off this so-called depression and tendency towards lower prices. Again I have to confess that I more or less agreed with them. I thought that was the situation, but it turned out not to be so. Some hon. members might say that the Korean war was the cause of that. But if the government of the day had gone into a program of public works, it would have laid itself wide open to criticism today, because the public works program is going to have to be cut down. I am not too critical of the opposition, Mr. Speaker, because it must be maddening to sit in the opposition and make statement after statement, only to find out that none of them turns out to be in accordance with the facts. They complain about the government not giving them any information. Under the circumstances I suggest that the government should give them some more information, so that when they make these assertions they will know what they are talking about.
I want to say a word about inflation. There is a great deal of talk about the man in the street and what a hard time he is having.


I can recall the time, in the thirties, when I started to farm in Saskatchewan. I had a hard time. It is true that the dollar is inflated today. Some people say that it takes two dollars now to buy what one would buy a few years ago. But I do not think it makes much difference to the average Joe, including the average farmer, whether the dollar goes only half as far as it used to, provided that he now has two or three instead of one. I think that is the picture throughout Canada today. I have not travelled over a great deal of Canada, but I have been around a little bit, and when I visit the towns and cities I do not go to the high-priced hotels. I visit my friends and relations who happen to live in the poorer parts of the city and quite close to the slums, if there are any. I find that today there is less difference between the poor man and the rich man than there has been at any previous time in the history of this country.
We have another group that are complaining about inflation. We have a certain number of people in this country who have bought insurance and government bonds and who have money in the bank. They are complaining because they thought at one time that the interest on those savings would keep them. They are in a bad way. I suggest to them that if they have not the standard of living they think they should have, they should spend a little of their principal in these days. If the principal will not keep them going, they have one consolation, Mr. Speaker. I am hopeful that we shall have the old age pension at seventy without a means test, and at sixty-five with a means test. If by that time they have not anything left, they can do as many of the rest of us may have to do, namely, live on the pension. If they will not be sixty-five at that time, then they can get out and work for a living as most of us Canadians do.
I am now going to turn to my final subject, and I wish to read a little poem I have here. I do not think the author was Shakespeare or Bobbie Burns or anyone of that calibre; he may have been one of my colleagues from the province of Ontario. It reads:
To the winging bird the only word is Tweet, tweet, tweet;
To the maid in spring the word she loves is Sweet, sweet, sweet;
But the damndest word X ever heard is Wheat, wheat, wheat.
I realize that to many hon. members wheat is not an interesting subject. I must confess that when hon. members are speaking about fish-and properly so, although I listen-I am not greatly interested. Since I represent a wheat-growing constituency, I am going to talk about wheat for a few minutes. Today in

-Canada, as most people know, wheat is handled through the Canadian wheat board. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the time will never come when I shall have to market my wheat in any other way. I want to make it very plain where I stand.
Some people argue that if we had an open market we would have received much higher prices for our wheat. That I question. I am going to use flax as an example, to show the house what happens on the open market. I think an open market is a crazy set-up. I harvested flax this fall, and therefore I am talking about something with which I am familiar. That is why I did not deal with external affairs. At the conclusion of the special session last fall 1 went home and got out the combine, and I threshed a fairly good crop of flax. As I said, I am using flax as an illustration to show the difference between the operations of the open market and those of the wheat board. I repeat that I am not in favour of the open market set-up. The law of supply and demand will definitely set what you are to get for a thing in the end, but I am not in favour of that method of marketing.
Coming back to flax, last fall while harvesting my flax I drew one load to the elevator. That was in October. I do not recall the date, but I sold it for $3.34 a bushel. It was the first grade of flax. The elevator man tested it for moisture, and it just got by. He said to me: "If it is tough tomorrow" -that was in the evening-"don't draw any in". The next day the sun did not come out, and I figured it might be tough, so I did not take it in. I put it in the granary and sold it in December before coming down here, and I received $4.70 a bushel for that flax. It was the same flax that I had sold for $3.34 a short time before. It has gone up since, and within recent days it has gone down. It dropped a matter of thirty cents a bushel in two days, fifteen cents a bushel a day. That is the same set-up as we had under the open-market scheme for wheat.
There are some hon. members who have made the statement-I do not know whether the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) is one of them but I know definitely that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is one of them-that the farmers had lost thirty-five cents a bushel under the wheat board set-up this fall. The price set by the board was $1.40. I do not think we lost thirty-five cents, because since then we have received twenty cents. The premier of our province has been running around the country and speaking over the radio, telling the western farmers that in Saskatchewan they have lost $100 million.
The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith If what he said was correct, then we have already received $56 million of that. That is what twenty fcents a bushel is going to amount to; and I am informed on very good authority that we can expect another twenty cents. Therefore we in the province of Saskatchewan are going to have under that scheme $12 million more than we lost.
I hear voices, Mr. Speaker, but I am not sure just where they are coming from.
In conclusion I wish to say that many of the farmers in western Canada are a little disappointed that the government has not seen fit to make an announcement on the five-year pool. It is true we have been told that negotiations are going on with the United Kingdom government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not according to the Prime Minister.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, discussion, if that suits the hon. member better. I do not care whether it is discussion or negotiation. I was going to say that I was getting sick and tired, but I am going to leave out the word "sick"; I am not sick yet but I may be a little tired. I am not blaming the government at the moment for not making the announcement. But I urge the government to crack the whip and get going on this negotiation or discussion with the United Kingdom government and let us have a decision on what is going to happen in respect to the five-year pool payments.
Many figures have been given as to what we should get. The other day the hon. member for Souris said that we should receive fifty cents a bushel as a final payment on the five-year pool, but that we were willing to take twenty-five cents. That is charitable. We are willing to take half of what we think we should get. If I may say so, I think tha+ thirty cents a bushel would be closer to the mark, and I agree with him that we are willing to take half, which in that case would be fifteen cents. Of course that is only my own opinion. If we were to demand the last cent from the United Kingdom government that we calculate we have lost under the agreement-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How about the Canadian government?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member had better get after them; I am talking about the other contract. If we were to demand the last cent from the United Kingdom government that we think we have lost, I think we would be a very mean people, particularly when we remember the battle of

The Address-Mr. Brooks Britain. We all know what Britain went through; but at the same time I do not think we should be expected to accept anything less than something in the neighbourhood of fifteen cents a bushel as a final payment. I would urge the government to do something before seeding time rolls around again or before Easter, about bringing this matter to a conclusion. I shall be going home at Easter, or at the end of the session. I have been following the session very closely, Mr. Speaker, and the policies of the government. I am prepared to go home and explain the policies of the government to my constituents. Unless we get something for this wheat I am not prepared to explain that; nor do I intend to make excuses.
We have a good strong government, and we are ready to support it. Once again I say we should have a settlement on this matter. However, I shall be speaking on this again, and if we get a settlement I think it should be in the neighbourhood of fifteen cents a bushel. I am prepared to make one of two addresses. If we get a fair payment, it will be a very pleasant and juicy address, but if there is nothing done, I can assure you, sir, that it will be sour and bitter.
I suppose that my colleagues and members of the opposition groups and some of the people in my constituency will say that I should not have said the things I have said; but I am quite sure that if they realize the consolation I get out of saying what I think, they will excuse me.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith) will pardon me if I did not follow his remarks very carefully. Unfortunately I could not hear the first part of his address. The second part of it had to do with wheat, which is not a matter of great interest to most members in the house, particularly those from the maritime provinces. I believe that in the sixteen years I have been here, practically fifty per cent of the time in debate has been taken up in the discussion of wheat.
For a few moments I should like to refer to the matter of controls. Two important matters have been before the house: first, our Canadian defence program, and second, controls and inflation. I shall not take much time in discussing inflation, because it was thoroughly covered by my leader yesterday. I will simply say that I agree one hundred per cent with the very practical ideas he expressed on the subject.
Contrary to what the hon. member who has just taken his seat may think, the people
TMr. Smith (Moose Mountain).]

of Canada are greatly exercised about controls and inflation. I believe that today it is the chief problem facing the people of this country, and certainly it is the problem which the people feel the government should deal with immediately. There is a feeling of impatience with the soaring of living costs throughout the country. Not only are the people impatient, but they have a genuine fear in their hearts about this condition.
Last night I listened to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and I must say that to a great extent I agree with his remarks. To illustrate a point he made, he mentioned his having paid sixty cents for a collar which only a short time before could have been bought for thirty cents. Let me tell the house about an experience of my own in that regard. I went to a shoe store to buy a pair of shoes. The clerk told me that only the day before, the price of that particular type of shoe had increased by $2.50. While I was in the store a man who worked in a factory in our town came in, in company with his two boys, with the intention of buying shoes. He asked the price, and when he was told that the price of shoes for his boys had increased by more than $2, he said that he felt he could not buy at that time. Knowing that I was coming to Ottawa to attend the session, he turned to me and said, "You people up there will have to do something about this matter. It is becoming impossible for me to clothe and feed my family and to pay my rent, because of the way in which prices are soaring".
I am sure the experience of this man is that of all heads of families throughout the country. The hon. member for Moose Mountain said, "Oh, these people can use up their principal." The people I am speaking about -and there are tens of thousands of them across the country-have no principal to use up. The hon. member went on to say that the rich and the poor are in much the same position. That is not correct. The poor man today has not sufficient money with which to buy the necessities of life. This is one reason why I feel that the government must do something now to halt price increases. It is being done in the United States.
The hon. member for Moose Mountain says that the C.C.F., Social Credit and Progressive Conservative parties are backing controls. I would point out to him that in the United States today it is felt that a measure of controls is necessary. In Canada we are proud to follow the United States in many things. I believe that in this matter as well we would be wise to do so.
In the situation that is developing I am sure some controls have become necessary. I do not think over-all control is required,

The Address-Mr. Brooks
but certainly controls are necessary to some extent. I believe that public support would be behind a measure of controls at this time -and we must have public support; otherwise enforcement would not be possible. Some measure of control would curb the extra momentum gained by inflation at every step.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) told us there were many interests which are opposed to controls. We know this to be true. We know, for instance, that the producer may be opposed to controls, and that many consumers are opposed to controls. This is always true in an economy where the supply of goods is reduced in relation to the supply of dollars. That is what is happening in Canada today, when civilian goods are being turned to military uses, with the resulting scarcity which is causing inflation. In view of the height to which prices have climbed, it seems clear that some measure of control should have been put on two or three months ago. For instance, we read only yesterday in the evening papers that coal had been increased in price by $1.75 a ton. Pick up a paper any day and you will find that prices are going up, not just a few cents, but in many instances by much larger amounts.
It is not my intention to discuss this matter further at the moment. All the evidence we have points to the fact that some measure of control must be exercised in Canada. I agree with the Minister of Finance that one way to help to stop inflation is to have heavy taxation. Unless we tax the people heavily, there can be no question that inflation will do so. These two might work together. I agree with the Minister of Finance that we must balance our budget. These things go hand in hand with controls, and if immediate action is taken it will be well for the people of this country.
The other question which is exercising the minds of our people is that of security and the part we should play in world events. Canadians are a proud people, and I am satisfied that they wish us to carry our full share of such defence measures as may be necessary to preserve the liberties we cherish. Speaking yesterday, one hon. member compared what was being done by Canada and by Great Britain. It was pointed out that while Great Britain had from 600,000 to a million men under arms-and he accepted the lower figure-Canada has only 60,000, showing a ratio of ten to one. This means that Great Britain, with a population slightly more than three times that of Canada, and with natural resources far inferior to those we have, has armed forces ten times as great as those of Canada.
There is the same ratio also in the United States. Much praise has been given the United States for the splendid work which is being done in Korea. We are all proud of our neighbours to the south for the action they have taken in that country. We feel that the United Nations took the only action that was possible. But it must be remembered that the United States was the only nation that had troops in that vicinity, and therefore she has had to bear a great burden there.
It must be remembered that while Great Britain has only one brigade in Korea, she has many thousands of troops in Malaya and a large army at Hong Kong. This is all part of the picture in the east. It should be pointed out also that France has a large army in Indo-China, which is part of the picture in the east. When we give great credit to the United States, as we should, for what she is doing in Korea, we must not forget the part that is being played by Great Britain and France in their respective areas.
Canada is going to spend $5,000 million in the next few years on defence. This is an enormous sum and should permit the raising and equipping of whatever troops are necessary. We should be able to produce the munitions that may be required. All sections of Canada are anxious to bear their fair and adequate share of the responsibility, both as to taxes and as to manpower. There is no question that every part of Canada will bear its share of taxes, because taxes are levied on the same basis all across the country.
If war should come and it is necessary for Canada to raise large forces, I think the people would wish that the raising of manpower be done in a way that will be fair to all sections of the country. Everybody knows that in time of war some men must fight, while others serve in other ways; and soldier and civilian morale will be much better if the selection for service is defined in the most understandable terms possible. I think the people of Canada wish and desire that that be done.
All sections of Canada-the maritimes, central Canada and the west-should have some share in the production of munitions and supplies. The minister has made much of the fact that equipment has been sent to Belgium and the Netherlands; that was a good thing and we approve of it. It was the logical and sensible thing to do. I am satisfied that since Canada is taking equipment from the United States we could not do less than send equipment to those people in Europe who will be fighting, if necessary, the battles of freedom.
I think also that the people of Canada approve of the defence of Europe. I have

The Address-Mr. Brooks heard very little talk of isolationism here in Canada, although there has been a good deal in the United States. I am thankful that we in Canada have not taken the same attitude as a great many people in the United States have taken, although it seems to be dying out. Everyone realizes that if the western hemisphere is to be defended, Europe also must be defended. One minister has said that if we should lose Europe to Russia in the next war we would lose one of the greatest manufacturing potentials in the world. We would lose all the steel and manufacturing centres to Russia. There is no reason in the world why Canadians should not approve the defence of Europe.
The question of arming Germany has come up. This is a difficult problem for the United Nations or others concerned to deal with. There is no doubt that eastern Germany is armed today. Russia has 50,000 east Germans under arms at the present time. They are equipped with tanks, guns and aeroplanes. If the other half of Germany is not armed, we may have the same situation as we had in Korea. The Russians armed the North Koreans while the United States left the South Koreans unarmed, Then they went away and the North Koreans moved into South Korea, and we all know the great difficulty our people have been having in trying to drive them back and to retain that country. So I think these matters, or most of them, have the approval of the Canadian people.
My main object in speaking this afternoon was not to touch on the matter of controls and the manpower problems that will arise should another war come, but to deal with another matter which is referred to in the speech from the throne, in the following words:
The urgent need of the St. Lawrence seaway and power project in relation to the security of this continent is becoming increasingly apparent. It is the view of my ministers that the Canadian authorities should be kept in a position to co-operate promptly in undertaking construction of the project once affirmative action has been taken by the appropriate United States authorities.
Anyone who has read the press of Canada and the United States during the last few weeks knows that the St. Lawrence seaway is a burning question in the United States. A bill has been introduced in congress by F. D. Roosevelt, Jr., a son of the late president, providing for the construction of the seaway and power project. In introducing the bill Mr. Roosevelt said:
The St. Lawrence seaway and power project will provide the least expensive means of providing necessary transportation of iron ore and other


critical materials and the least costly way of providing additional power-so badly needed in New York, New England and eastern Canada.
President Truman has said that it is necessary to construct this seaway for the national security of the United States and Canada. As one from the maritimes it is my opinion that the St. Lawrence seaway will be of absolutely no benefit to the people of the maritime provinces. However, I do not mean that the people of the maritime provinces will object to the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. When our government and the government of the United States decide that the seaway is necessary for the defence of this continent we shall have no choice in the matter but to support it. Nevertheless, as I have said, as a peacetime project it would be of practically no benefit to the people of the maritimes. As a matter of fact it would be a hindrance, because there is no doubt that the main reason for constructing the St. Lawrence waterway would be to provide a great deal of additional electrical power to Ontario and Quebec; and the more power they have, the more industry will be concentrated in those provinces, to the detriment of the maritimes and the west. However, on the basis on which it probably will be constructed, as I said a moment ago we in the maritimes do not feel that we can raise any great objection.
In fairness to the people of our province, however, there is another project I should like to mention. It is also an international project, of interest both to the United States and to Canada. I refer to the development of hydroelectric power in Passamaquoddy bay and the bay of Fundy. This is not new; it has been advocated for a great many years, and has been investigated at different times. I remember that some twenty years ago the matter was discussed in the New Brunswick house when I was a member there; and while the Americans of that day were more or less in favour of it, we in Canada were opposed. The chief opposition at that time came from the fishermen of that area, who said it would ruin their industry. That idea now has been exploded, and engineers have reported very favourably on the feasibility of the project. Mr. Truman also favours it. As far back as last April an Associated Press dispatch from Washington said:
Mr. Truman was described today as favouring revival of the Passamaquoddy-Maine tidal power project.
Senator Brewster and Senator Smith of Maine and many other statesmen of the New England states also favour this project. What it would mean to the people of the maritime provinces, and particularly to the people of

New Brunswick, cannot be overestimated. At the outset it would mean a million horsepower divided between the New England states and the maritime .provinces. It would mean that our province would be placed on an equal footing with other sections of Canada so far as hydro power is concerned. If, therefore, the government of Canada feels that it must go through with the St. Lawrence seaway, in justice to the people of the maritime provinces, who in years past have contributed many millions toward the cost of projects in other parts of Canada and who would have to pay their share of the cost of constructing the St. Lawrence seaway, I think it is only fair that consideration be given the development of this international power project in Passamaquoddy bay, which would mean so much to our people.

speechtext:
Yes; but one thing at a time. I should like to quote what the maritime board of trade has to say about this project, as contained in a report appearing in the Moncton Times a few months ago:
Low Cost Power is New Brunswick's Need
In the lengthy and important agenda which the maritime board of trade went through in executive session here, that regarding the projected harnessing of the tides of Passamaquoddy bay transcended all other features in so far as the future development of New Brunswick is concerned.
This is a prodigious scheme, greater than any other power project ever undertaken in the mari-times, and, if given the green light by United States congress and the Canadian parliament as a joint enterprise of the two neighbour nations, would mean an illimitable surge in the industrial and commercial expansion of New Brunswick and also a very large section of Prince Edward Island. Both these provinces have been greatly retarded in economic progress, because the natural resources in New Brunswick, capable of producing more than a sufficiency of electrical energy in continuous supply for an inestimable time and at low cost, have never been capitalized upon.
Then the last paragraph:
It is indeed encouraging that a favourable report is in prospect-
That report is not only in prospect; it has been submitted.
-as ensuing from the recent investigations conducted by the international joint commission into the projected development of electric power from 'Quoddy tides, and that consequent upon such a report there exists the strong possibility of future joint Canadian-American action to implement it. The completion of this scheme would surely witness the ushering in of an era that New Brunswick has long looked forward to as being a hive of industry and the scene of busy commercial enterprises of various types.
That pretty well expresses the opinion of the people of the maritime provinces. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Saint
The Address-Mr. Brooks John-Albert (Mr. Riley) on his excellent speech of a few days ago. He mentioned something which I am sure he would not claim to be new, because it has been mentioned in this house by myself and other maritime members on many occasions. I refer to the decentralization of industry in this dominion. During the last war I brought this matter to the attention of the government, and at that time the minister told me the main reason we could not have industry in the maritime provinces was that we did not have the hydroelectric power. Since that time we have developed new sources of power in the maritimes, and today are in a position to take on these small industries which were mentioned a few days ago by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. If the government would carry out this extensive power development in Passamaquoddy bay, however, we could not only take on small industries; we could take on extensive industries as well.
We have been the neglected section of Canada. This is an old story, and I suppose many hon. members are tired of listening to it. But we have been sadly neglected. In the last war only one-half of one per cent of our war industry came to my province of New Brunswick. It was an absolute disgrace. Only two per cent came to the whole of the maritime provinces. Now we are threatened with another great war. Whether or not that war comes-and I sincerely hope it does not- billions of dollars are to be spent in the production of munitions and other military supplies, and surely it is time that we in the maritimes, who have always done our full share in supplying manpower for the defence and development of Canada, should receive more consideration from this government and the country in general.
My hon. friend spoke about manpower. We have the manpower in the maritime provinces, but unfortunately it does not stay there. Just this morning the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) was telling me about seventeen young men who left the small village of Centreville in Carle-ton county in one day, to come to Ontario to look for work. I know that young men are leaving my own town daily, and I am sure the hon. member for Saint John-Albert knows of the hundreds who are leaving his city to come to Ontario and Quebec to find employment. A few days ago we had the great privilege of visiting the Canadair factory at Cartierville on the island of Montreal. I enjoyed that trip. There we saw thousands of young men. It was a regular hive of industry. We were told that there were 5,300 men working in that one factory.

The Address-Mr. Brooks I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that there are more men working in that one factory in the city of Montreal on government work than there are in the whole of the three maritime provinces. I do not think it is necessary to argue this point any further, but I do hope this government will realize that we in these provinces are deserving of more consideration.
During the last war we trained many men in the maritimes. There was a splendid camp at my home town of Sussex, New Brunswick; another one at Debert, one at Aldershot and one at Utopia. I was amazed, as was the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), to learn that all our men are now being sent to Fort Lewis in Washington for training. That might have been necessary when those men were being trained as a brigade, but why is it necessary now when we have all the space that we have in Canada to train our own soldiers? I recall that before the last war Great Britain wanted to train some airmen in Canada, and that move was opposed in this house because some members were afraid that Canada would lose her sovereignty if she allowed the troops of another country to come here to train. I have not heard of the United States losing her sovereignty because we sent a few thousand troops over there to train.
However, Mr. Speaker, that is beside the point. The point I wish to make is that since the maritimes have been so badly neglected in other matters, I see no reason why, when we shall be training a good many soldiers for some years to come, the camps at Sussex, Aldershot and other places should not be rebuilt. There is a good nucleus there for a start, and the men could be trained there.
I was amazed to hear that the men who were training at Fort Lewis received an extra $20 per month, and that the officers received an extra $40 per month, because they were training outside of our country. These extra payments amount to something like $200,000 a month for 8,000 men training in this area. The minister is not in his seat, but I should like to know just how much we are paying the United States authorities for the privilege of training our men in Washington. I venture to say that it runs into a tidy sum. I venture to say that the government could rebuild these camps in Sussex and other parts of the maritime provinces for the amount of money they are paying and will pay for having these men trained in the United States.
I listened with attention and interest to the speech delivered yesterday by the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), because he mentioned a matter which is very close to us in the province of New Brunswick, and


that is the question of the conversion of our forests into pulpwood, one of the chief industries in New Brunswick. The price of pulp this winter has been so high, and the United States newsprint people have been so anxious to buy it, that almost every standing tree is being cut down for pulp. I feel that we are using up a heritage that belongs to the people who come after us. When the hon. member for Comox-Alberni mentioned the fact that each copy of a recent issue of a United States newspaper weighed three and three-quarter pounds, we were given some idea of the terrible waste. Trees that could be cut down later to make lumber are now going to the United States to be used for this purpose. It is about time something was done about it. I believe it would be preferable to send this pulp to Great Britain or some of the European countries where the newspapers contain only three or four pages. I would rather have a British paper of three or four pages, so far as real news is concerned, than some of these bulky twenty-five and thirty-page editions from the United States which contain a lot of trash. It is a shameful waste of pulp and of the forests of Canada.
I have some other notes here, Mr. Speaker, but I feel that I have spoken long enough. I wish to thank you for your kind attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all join with those hon. members who have congratulated the mover (Mr. McMillan) and the seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The manner in which these two hon. members acquitted themselves has brought honour not only to them but also to the constituencies which they represent. I also want to join with the member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) in the high words of praise which he had for the newly appointed minister from Alberta, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham). Those of us who know the minister have been struck by his sincerity of purpose, his business ability, and above all his honesty. Some of us who know him quite well often refer to him as "honest George."
The speech from the throne has been significant in that it has conveyed to the people of Canada the fact that an emergency situation now exists in view of the further deterioration in the international field. The policy of our government, and the desire of the Canadian people, is to prevent war and maintain peace. However, the international tension today has been caused by communist imperialism in its determination to dominate the world by force or by the fear of force. We in Canada, and the people of the

free world, are compelled to take such steps in our national defence as may be adequate to safeguard our security.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) pointed out to us a few days ago what the government's national defence policy will mean to the Canadian taxpayer in dollars and cents. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has indicated .some of the sacrifices which will be expected of the Canadian people. The same thing may be said of the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) with regard to housing.
It is my intention in this debate to deal exclusively with the international situation. I might as well warn hon. members in this house, as well as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), that some of the views which I shall express are probably different from some which have been expressed on this topic in this chamber. At the outset I feel that the difficult position in which we find ourselves today is, to a considerable extent, our own fault. When I say "our own fault", I mean the fault of the democratic countries towards whom the world looks for leadership and guidance in international affairs. It is true that when we fought the last war we defeated Hitlerism; but it would appear that we did not lay the foundations of a lasting peace. I think that the blame falls on the democratic world in that we failed to assess international communism and that at the same time we allowed another dictator to obtain tremendous powers, the like of which have never before been witnessed in the history of mankind. If we assess communism, we find that Marxist communism is a militant philosophy based on struggle. Because of the nature of its inspiring promises, it creates fanatics within its ranks. It is a philosophy that will not tolerate any criticism or stand for any opposition and therefore it cannot be appeased. Marxist communism is based on the teaching of the German philosopher Hegel who said that when you have two conflicting views or two opposing ideologies as between states, such differences can only be settled by war.
Let us face the facts. The world today is divided into two camps, with two opposing ideologies; our western world with our way of life and the communistic world which is being headed by the Kremlin. We can therefore ask ourselves this question. If my appraisal of the communist philosophy is correct, are we to expect that the communist leaders throughout the world, including Stalin and the fanatics in his ranks, will change their methods and mend their ways
The Address-Mr. Decore even if we match them plane for plane and soldier for soldier? The question is: Can a leopard change its spots?
Let me point out that it is not so much international communism with which we are obliged to contend as it is in effect with Russian imperialism. It is evident to all of us that international communism is merely being used by Stalin as a tool or instrument to further his own imperialistic designs. I repeat that it was a failure of the free world to assess communism in its true light and in allowing Stalin to obtain vast powers, many of them through default, that makes our .position now most difficult. However, this is now water under the bridge.
The Korean incident, although regrettable in that it has caused great sacrifices especially on the part of our good neighbour to the south, has nevertheless awakened the free world to the danger of international communism and Russian imperialism. The pattern of Stalin's operations should be clear to all of us by now. Although there may be a cease-fire in Korea, we must be prepared to face similar difficulties in other parts of the world. Only yesterday, I believe, Anthony Eden, in making a statement at Westminster, warned the world of grave possibilities in Yugoslavia in the near future.
Analogies are trick bases for argument, but the fact is that communism has many heads; and it is necessary to recognize the difficulties of the problem of destroying it. In Greek mythology many of us have heard of the hydra-headed monster which Hercules was given the task of destroying. I recall reading in the New York Times an editorial which appealed to me-incidentally it is dated October 25, 1950-and which reads in part as follows:
This simultaneous activity at opposite poles of the earth is a reminder of the hydra-headed character of international communism. It might be well for us to remember, too, that the heads of the mythical snake grew back again as fast as Hercules cut them off. He had to root out its body and destroy the one immortal head (shall we say the Kremlin?) before the monster was defeated.
Let us not forget that communism or communist imperialism is centred today in Moscow. Let us therefore, now that we realize the menace of communism and of Russian imperialism, be prepared to deal with our potential enemy effectively. Let us not underestimate his strength; but above all let us not overlook his weakness.
When I say that we must not underestimate the enemy's strength, I mean that certainly we must not underestimate the strength of the Red army, the strategic position of the

The Address-Mr. Decore soviet bloc and the aggressive leadership of international communism throughout the world. Certainly tanks, guns and planes are necessary and vital in our defence preparations. Should we be forced into it, there is no easy way to fight Soviet Russia, but I think Hitler has shown us the hard way of doing so. Let us not fall into that fallacy which lay at the root of Hitler's stupidity when he thought that Soviet Russia could be beaten by military means alone. Probably I should modify that statement and say that perhaps Soviet Russia can be beaten by military means alone but at a terrible price.
When the nazis launched their attack on Soviet Russia, they met with such huge successes at first that it was almost unbelievable. Hundreds of thousands of men laid down their arms and surrendered to the Germans. The population welcomed the Germans, not because they had any love for the nazis but because they looked upon them as liberators from the Kremlin oppressors. It was only after Hitler treated these people in the same brutal fashion as he treated the Jews that the population turned against him, with the results that were indicated in the battle of Stalingrad.
What is this weakness in Soviet Russia's empire today which we must not overlook and which we must be prepared to capitalize on? Many people in Canada and throughout the free world do not fully appreciate the fact that within the borders of Soviet Russia there are about one hundred ethnic groups, the most numerous being the Russians themselves. The Russians, however, comprise less than half of the total population in the U.S.S.R.; and during the time of the czars and during the time of Stalin they have been the motivating or driving force of the nation. Their dominance over the smaller minorities, however, has been made possible because of their superiority in numbers; but it has always been resented by those smaller minorities.
May I say that the apparent unity which exists in the Soviet union today has been made possible through slave camps, liquidations and mass extermination of racial, ethnical and religious groups as such. We can feel quite certain that the rulers in the Kremlin, in order to maintain further unity within their borders or that so-called unity within the Soviet union, must resort to further mass exilings, slave camps and liquidations. The national problems of the Soviet are one of their most vulnerable spots. We can, I think, rely on these suppressed people to be the most certain allies of democracy against the Red tyranny.

Let us also bear in mind the fact that today there are millions of political prisoners in concentration camps and under slave labour conditions. There are today throughout the Soviet union hundreds of thousands of families, one or more of whose members have either been liquidated or sent to slave camps for political reasons.
The fact is that in spite of nearly two generations of indoctrination, despite the mass exilings and mass liquidations, despite the slave camps and the dread secret police to crush all opposition, there is a bitter resentment against Stalin's regime. That, Mr. Speaker, is where is to be found the enemy's weakest spot-in that smouldering opposition of the population against its oppressors in the Kremlin, which once aroused can become a weapon in our favour much more effective than the atom bomb itself.
And what about the satellite states such as Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria, Roumania and Czechoslovakia? Apart from Titoism, which is prevalent within the communist ranks itself, there is evidence of a strong but latent underground, an opposition which is smouldering but waiting for an opportunity.
The menace of the Soviets to freedom' is realized by the democratic world but it is also important that the Soviet's weakness should receive attention. It is already receiving attention from prominent men throughout the world and among them is Harold E. Stassen, president of the university of Pennsylvania, and a prominent Republican, who in a radio address over the national network made this statement. Incidentally his observations were based on a trip that he made around the world. He said, as reported in the New York Times of January 16, 1951:
First of all I received information all around the outside of the vast communist empire of the discontent and unrest within the Soviet union and within the iron curtain countries. This includes the red army itself.
According to the New York Times he urged the United States to rearm and called for solid support of General Dwight D. Eisenhower. He also urged a revision of the United States foreign policy, and sought certain goals. I quote further from the New York Times:
The establishment of separate national sovereignty and true independence of the Ukraine, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Roumania, Bulgaria and Hungary.
The release of all of the millions of political prisoners now in concentration camps and under forced labour in the Soviet union.
The granting of the Russian lands to the Russian peasants for their own farming.

The granting of the right of genuine labour unions to organize and bargain collectively everywhere in the world. The winning of the right of all the people to worship God as they choose.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a very inspiring message to those millions of people behind the iron curtain. It gives them new hope and new encouragement. It hits at the very heart of Stalin's brutal tyranny. How much more effective this message would be if it was the official policy of the United States, of Canada and of the free world?
Canada of course does not decide the United States foreign policy nor that of the United Kingdom. But it is one of the member states of the North Atlantic treaty. From the observations I made while being associated with the recent Canadian delegation to the United Nations assembly, I realized the tremendous role that Canada does play in international affairs, and realized also the weight exerted and the ability recognized by delegates to the United Nations from throughout the world of our own Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).
Someone would say that this type of policy which I call "political warfare" if adopted, shall we say by Canada and the western democracies, would offend Mr. Stalin. No doubt it will offend Mr. Stalin. It is a weak spot in his armour, but let us not forget that he has left no stone unturned through the use of the communist international organization, the cominform, to rouse and whip up fifth columnists and traitors in Canada and other countries; to create fear and unrest. One of his most effective weapons against the world in creating fear and distrust has been the use by him of this so-called political warfare.
Let us turn the tables on him and give him back some of his own medicine. Let us offer new hope and new encouragement to those millions behind the iron curtain who are our potential allies, by supporting them in what we believe in and what is the very foundation of democracy, namely, freedom.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, along with previous speakers, I wish to congratulate both the mover (Mr. McMillan) and the seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am sure each did credit to himself and to the constituents whom he represents.
The point at issue in the debate at the moment is the C.C.F amendment which has been moved by the hon member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), asking the immediate reimposition of price controls and the payment of subsidies where necessary so as to protect the health and living standards of the Canadian people.
The Address-Mr. Argue
I listened with great attention to the speech of the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith). He said that he would support our amendment had we included in it the provision that wages should also be controlled.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the provision for the control of wages is already part of the amendment, as it has been moved. It says:
. . . the immediate reimposition of price controls ... so as to project the health and living standards of the Canadian people.
To my mind price controls mean prices of all commodities, including wages. We ask that controls shall be implemented in such a way as to protect the health and living standards of the Canadian people We suggest therefore by those words that any control of wages or any control of farm prices that would stem from the adoption of this amendment shall be control in a fair and equitable manner.
Then the hon. member for Moose Mountain went on to say that he was a member of the farmers' union. I took down his words. He said: "If the farmers' union will support controls I too will support controls." I should like to read to him a resolution which was passed at the most recent annual convention of the Saskatchewan Farmers' Union held in Saskatoon between the dates of December 12 and December 15. The resolution reads as follows:
Whereas we, the members of the farmers' union, view with alarm the general economic trend wherein prices in general are sure to be increased, and are convinced that security lies in price control,
Therefore be it resolved that we demand that the federal government put price controls in effect at a point comparable with farm prices.
This resolution proves beyond doubt that the farmers' union are solidly behind price control. I suggest to the hon. member for Moose Mountain that we shall welcome now his support of our amendment asking for price controls, since the Saskatchewan Farmers' Union, of which he is a member, is supporting price controls at this time.
Last night I listened with attention to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) elaborate upon and enumerate the various fiscal and monetary measures the government had already taken to deal with inflation. He suggested that those measures were getting at the root cause of inflation, and suggested further that this was no time to implement over-all price controls.
The best way for one to judge whether those monetary and fiscal measures have been and are effective is to look over the price increases in the last twelve months and compare those increases with the increase in the cost of living index in the twelve months immediately
318	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Argue preceding the imposition of price controls in 1941. In looking over that index one finds that while it increased by 8 [DOT] 1 points between September 1940 and September 1941, and while the government following that increase felt it was necessary to have over-all price controls, the increase in the price index between January 1950 and January 1951 has been, not 8-1 points but 11-5 points. In other words, if there was any reason to impose price controls in 1941-and there was-then there is even greater reason today.
The degree of inflation rampant in the Canadian economy today and for the past twelve months is even greater than the degree of inflation which prevailed prior to the government's imposing over-all price controls in the fall of 1941.
Last night the minister seemed to take great exception to the suggestion put forth by the .leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that because of inflation our government bonds were no longer the same safe and secure investment they had once been. It seems to me that, with the runaway inflation as we have it today, many Canadians will consider seriously cashing their bonds and discontinuing the purchase of bonds as a method of saving.
One has but to look at what has happened in the last five years to the value of the dollars Canadians have invested in government bonds to see that there are many investments which have been much more secure. In January 1946 the cost of living index was 119-9; five years later, in January 1951, it had increased to 172-5. The purchasing power of a $100 bond bought in January 1946, according to the government's cost of living index, is today only $69.52, on the basis of 1946 prices.	.
So that anyone who bought a $100 bond in January, 1946, and cashed it in January of 1951 would find that instead of getting $100 in value, the $100 they would obtain would buy goods to the value of only $69.52, on the basis of 1946 prices. In other words, anyone who invested $100 in government bonds in January, 1946, has in the last five years lost $31.48 in purchasing power. If the bond had been a Canada savings bond, always worth one hundred cents on the dollar as a monetary value, the interest in those five years would have amounted to $13.75. Therefore anyone who purchased a bond five years ago and cashes it today finds his net loss, after deducting interest, amounts to $17.73, in relation to purchasing power.
I make the statement that any time the value of the Canadian dollar goes down


faster than the rate of interest on our bonds, then at that point our bonds cease to be a safe, secure, sound and attractive investment. The minister said that during the session last fall, and since that time, the government has been getting at the root causes of inflation by drawing in some of the excess purchasing power.
One of the measures I presume the minister would advance in support of his contention that there has been an effort to reduce the supply of money in the country would be the small, the almost insignificant, increase in the corporation tax, amounting to an additional 5 per cent. That in itself, as events have proven, is not, I am afraid, an antiinflationary measure of any real strength. At the session last fall the government failed to take one of the most important fiscal measures that I believe-and I said it at that time- they should have taken. That is, there should have been not increases in the sales tax on soft drinks, /chocolate bars and chewing gum, but a substantial increase in the income tax as it affects the people in the higher income brackets.
If any tax can be considered fair, and based upon ability to pay, then surely it must be a properly graduated income tax. But the government did nothing last fall to draw off the excess purchasing power in the hands of the well-to-do people in Canada. At the same time it did not hesitate to ask for and to implement the authority it was given to curtail instalment buying. It has not hesitated at this session to increase the amount of the down payment to build a house under the National Housing Act.
I am opposed to any legislation similar to the increase in down payments on instalment buying or the increase in down payments under the National Housing Act, when such provisions are drafted in such a way that they merely prevent the lowest income groups from making necessary purchases. I say the type of legislation we have for the curtailment of instalment buying, and the announcement with respect to down payments under the National Housing Act, taken in the light of the fact that as yet there has been no increase in the income tax levied against the well-to-do, is nothing short of class legislation.
I have here an editorial appearing in the Co-operative Consumer, the official publication of the various consumer co-operatives throughout Saskatchewan. Those associations are composed of tens of thousands of members throughout the western provinces, most of whom are farmers. The editorial says this:
The imposition of credit controls is intended to reduce the demand for certain classes of consumer

goods among the Canadian people. It is expected that this decreased demand will tend to halt the present trend toward inflation but those who favour the credit restrictions fail to see that these restrictions do not limit purchases by persons of wealth. Indeed, such credit restrictions are a subtle type of economic class privilege since only the poor people may be unable to make the necessary down payments and unable to complete payment for major items in the limited term allowed for such payment. Rich men and rich women can still buy at their pleasure. The wife of the poorly paid labourer, teacher, pastor or other worker, may have to forget her dreams of a new refrigerator or a new washing machine. The struggling young couples with their young families see their only chance to secure many of those things which make life worthwhile vanish with the introduction of anti-poor credit controls. The regrettable feature of the whole credit control situation lies in the fact that these credit controls establish the principle of economic class legislation-*
I agree wholeheartedly with the sentiments expressed in that editorial. The editorial goes on to suggest certain methods that might have been used in place of this so aptly termed class legislation. The editor states that if the government had desired to cut down the purchase of new automobiles in a fair and equitable manner it might have established a permit system which would not allow anyone driving an automobile of a model say later than 1945 to purchase a new car. Or it might have required permits for the purchase of refrigerators, washing machines and so on, which would make them available only to mothers of families. I think that type of allocation of scarce consumer goods would be more in the interests of the Canadian people and the cause for which we are raising such a large army, navy and air force than legislation which has the effect of pushing even lower the standard of living of thousands of people who cannot afford to pay 20 per cent down when they purchase a new refrigerator or make a down payment twice as large as that previously required under the National Housing Act.
I want now to discuss the effects of price controls on farmers and their attitude toward price controls. If I can interpret their resolutions correctly the farmers of Canada do not want an over-all price freeze on every single item of goods the farmer sells or goods the farmer produces at current prices, but they are asking for price controls which will mean parity prices for the farmer, parity prices for the worker and will permit-

speechtext:
I come now to the question of how much the government should pay as a final payment on the five-year pool. I notice the hon. member for Moose Mountain, the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) and the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) have advocated a payment in the neighbourhood of 15 cents per bushel. I shduld like to refer the hon. member for Moose Mountain to another resolution passed by the Saskatchewan Farmers Union of which he says he is a member-since he says he will support their demands for price controls. I should not hesitate to support their demands in connection with a final payment on the five-year pool demanding a settlement on the basis of not less than $2 per bushel, basis No. 1, Fort William. If that resolution were implemented it would have the effect of providing a final payment of 25 cents per bushel on the five-year pool.
Lest there be any misunderstanding in any quarter of this house or of the country, let me say that I support foursquare the demands of the Saskatchewan Farmers Union, the Alberta Farmers Union, the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities, the Alberta wheat pool, other farm organizations and individual farmers who have written to me all demanding a payment of 25 cents per bushel. To date I have received no resolution passed by any group of farmers saying that they would be satisfied with a payment of 15 cents per bushel. Rather I have had many resolutions from farm organizations and from local groups of farmers saying that, if anything less than 25 cents per bushel is paid, farmer delegations will be in Ottawa shortly afterward demanding a further payment until the total payment is at least 25 cents per bushel.
On August first there was a drop in the initial price of 35 cents per bushel, followed by a lack of box cars and a lack of marketing facilities. All these things taken together have resulted in my opinion in reducing support for the policies the government has directed the wheat board to follow.
Farm organizations and the vast majority of farmers support the wheat board and ask that its powers be extended to cover the handling of oats, barley, flax and rye.
When the government is considering the final payment they should take a number of factors into account. Last fall the initial price dropped 35 cents per bushel. Our crop

The Address-Mr. Argue was severely frosted and the spreads were increased to the point where the price of feed wheat at the local elevator point was 80 cents odd per bushel. And when the farmer tried to market his wheat he was told there was a shortage of box cars, that most of our box cars were in the United States. The government, the board of transport commissioners and the railroad companies all taken together could not get enough box cars to handle the shipment of last fall's crop.
We used to have a quota system which worked very well. That was followed conscientiously by the wheat board and supported by farmers. But this fall the quota system seemed to literally break down. An eight-bushel quota was first established at most points. At a great many local delivery points, long before the eight-bushel quota was filled the quota was lifted. At my neighbouring elevator point of Dahinda the elevators plugged up on the Thursday before Thanksgiving day. At that time farmers had delivered only approximately half the eight-bushel quota; yet the following morning the elevator agents received wires from the wheat board lifting the quota. The farmers were disappointed and angry. At that time many had not sold a single bushel of the 1950 crop, and even today in that area I know a number of farmers who have not sold any of their 1950 crop.
I believe in the quota system but I think it should be applied fairly, and should be maintained at our local elevator points until almost every farmer has delivered his full quota. I do not know the reason for the situation which prevailed at Moose Jaw this fall, but I know that situation provoked a great deal of criticism in an area of perhaps a hundred miles around that city. I was told Moose Jaw had a quota of twenty bushels per acre; I have been told since that it had no quota at all. If there was a quota at Moose Jaw, certainly it was a large one. At the same time early last fall all the towns on the Soo line, the towns on the C.N.R. line south of Moose Jaw and the towns along the C.P.R. line west -of Weyburn, had small quotas and very few box cars. So farmers trucked their wheat to Moose Jaw from up to seventy-five miles away because their local elevators could not handle the grain. We had the spectacle of farmers hiring truckers and paying twelve to fifteen cents a bushel to have their grain hauled to elevators seventy-five miles away because the elevators within two or three miles were full and could not handle their crops. I believe the distribution of box cars should have been handled

in such a way as to give the farmers adjacent to each delivery point a chance to market at least a reasonable proportion of their 1950 crop.
We are asking for a final payment of 25 cents a bushel under the five-year pool. That will amount to a great deal of money. Some of those who have taken part in this debate have agreed with the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith), who spoke this afternoon, and have said the Canadian government should crack the whip over the British government and make them come through with a further payment. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was in London last year, and when he came back he had something to say about the negotiation in which he had participated concerning the "have regard to" clause. This is what he said at page 3221 of Hansard for June 5, 1950:
We asked the United Kingdom what further settlement it is to make on account of the "have regard to" clause. The United Kingdom government took a very strong position that they had filled all obligations under that clause, and so far as the United Kingdom was concerned. We agreed on behalf of Canada that considering all the circumstances that was the case.
From that quotation we see that according to our own minister, in June of last year the British government had fulfilled the "have regard to" clause of the wheat agreement. The farmers of western Canada took exception to that statement. They are not demanding that the British government only shall make the payment of 25 cents per bushel. They are saying to the government of Canada, "As our agents for the marketing of our wheat over a five-year period, we think you should see that the "have regard to" clause is fulfilled. If in your wisdom you think the British government has fulfilled that clause, then we believe you should make up the difference between the final surplus in the wheat pool account and the 25 cent payment we are asking-if necessary out of the national treasury". So I say to the government that the farmers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are asking a final payment of 25 cents , a bushel; and they are asking this government to take whatever steps are necessary to see that this final payment is forthcoming.
I believe certain changes should be made in the wheat board act and in the policy which has been followed by the wheat board. I welcome the 20 cent increase in the initial prices for wheat and barley and the increase of 10 cents in the initial price for oats; but when that announcement was made I believe a statement should have been issued showing the present financial position

of the wheat board so the farmers would have, a reasonable idea what the final payment at the end of the year would be after the crop had been marketed. Further, I believe the annual report of the wheat board should be made public within three months of the end of the crop year, again in order that the farmers of the west may know the financial position of the wheat board and the amount of money they may expect to receive in further payments.
In asking for a final payment of 25 cents per bushel the farmers are calling upon the federal government to make up part of that amount out of the national treasury, because throughout the five-year pool the Canadian consumer obtained wheat at a price lower than was received for class II wheat on the world market. Farmers know that the cheap flour and bread policy of the government was not paid for in the main out of the national treasury, but was paid for by a few thousand prairie farmers. Today the farmers of western Canada are still subsidizing the Canadian consumer. For wheat sold in Canada and going into the production of flour the millers of this country are paying at present about $1.90 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William, which is the ceiling under the international wheat agreement. At the same time class II wheat is being sold in world markets at $2.12 per bushel. So on every bushel of Canadian wheat going into Canadian consumption the farmers of the west are subsidizing the Canadian consumer to the extent of 22 cents. I object to a policy of that kind. I do not object to wheat being sold1 at $1.90 per bushel or less; but if the Canadian consumer is to get cheap wheat let it be at the expense of all the people of Canada, not at the expense of one section of our population, in this case our wheat farmers.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, once again I urge upon the government the necessity of making a final payment of 25 cents a bushel under the five-year pool, and making that payment immediately.
