Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with all previous speakers in congratulating the mover (Mr. McMillan) and seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on their excellent speeches. I was particularly struck with the remarks of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) in referring to the contributory health plan to meet the cost of major accidents and sicknesses. I feel sure all members of this house are in accord with that idea, and I trust that the hon. member will keep on putting his plan forward until the government sees fit to adopt it.
The Address-Mr. Higgins
The accent so far in this debate has been on external affairs. I trust that I will be pardoned if I refer to Newfoundland matters for a short time. I do so because some of them have a bearing on the international situation. In that connection I refer to Gander airport, about which you have heard so much as the crossroads of the world, and the extension of the runways that is now contemplated. I wish to thank the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) for finally acceding to the request for the extension of these runways. I have a number of questions on the order paper one of which concerns the materials to be used in the new construction. However, at this time I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Transport to the fact that the runways are macadam now, and from the experience of those operating the planes at Gander it would appear necessary that the new construction, indeed, the whole of the runways, should be of concrete.
Recently one of the managers told me that in landing heavy aircraft such as the Boeing Stratospheres at certain times, the runways give the impression of being composed of snow. The planes would weave around. As I have said during other sessions, if Gander is going to be forced again into the position of being vital to the defence of the free world, then we have to have these runways in such condition that they will be able to carry the heavy war planes that will be put in use.
When speaking of Gander I should like also to draw the attention of the minister concerned to the condition of Goose airport. As hon. members will realize, Goose is probably the most strategic airport for the defence of the western world. I am not in a position to give any description of the condition or length of the runways of this airport, but I trust that those concerned will see to it that if extensions or repairs are required they will be undertaken before the need becomes too urgent.
There is one other factor in connection with Gander that I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport, and that concerns an organization in Newfoundland that is known as NONIA, Newfoundland Outport Nursing and Industrial Organization. This is a philanthropic body that has been in operation for some twenty-five years, and which is today primarily concerned with the weaving and knitting of wearable goods of high quality. The materials are distributed to various people throughout the province who make some little extra money in their spare time by knitting or weaving these woollen goods. One of the main places NONIA had for the sale of these goods was
322	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Higgins at Gander airport, where a display counter was maintained and a considerable amount of goods sold. Since the Department of Transport took over the airport, NONIA has been completely removed from Gander.
The other day the NONIA committee for this year issued a report in which there is a paragraph reading as follows:
It is with regret we report a complete "shut-out" for our goods at the Gander terminal. Last year, while the booth was under government supervision, we sold $3,000 worth but now that the concession has been given to a private firm, we are completely overlooked. It is to be deplored that such high-class goods, handiwork of Newfoundlanders, are banned from this important selling centre, where wide publicity could be given.
In that connection I may say that within the past year the government of Newfoundland had Mr. Leo Dolan, who is chief of the Canadian travel bureau, make a survey of Newfoundland tourist requirements. In Mr. Dolan's recently released report there appears this paragraph:
I saw, to my amazement, some of the handicraft progress already made in your island. The merchandising of these handicrafts should become a very profitable business. You have a handicraft industry that has a remarkable potentiality. I recommend that steps be taken to make the airport the show window of Newfoundland. I think all Newfoundland handicrafts ought to be on display.
Mr. Speaker, as you are aware Newfoundland is again trying to develop its tourist industry. One of the important phases of that tourist industry is naturally the display and sale of Newfoundland goods. As I have said, one of the chief outlets has been lost. It is easy to see why it would be the chief outlet because there are 1,400 passengers daily passing through Gander from all over the world. It is one of the greatest show windows we have for these goods, and it is closed. I would urge the Minister of Transport that immediate steps be taken whereby NONIA will be permitted to display and sell these goods at the airport.
I have another "thank you" to make, and this time it is to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), for his interest in promoting the increased sale of Bell island iron ore. As the minister is aware, we have had a number of questions back and forth in the house during past sessions about this matter, and I feel he has taken an active part in the recent sales increases. The operating company, Dosco, has announced its intention of making improvements in the handling and mining facilities which will cost about $6 million. It is said that the greatest labouring force in Bell island's history will be working there within a short time.
In thanking the minister for that, I am sure that he will appreciate that when the Greeks bear gifts they look for something


else. I am not asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce this time, but I am asking the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) if he will recall my request to him some time ago concerning the condition of the wharf at Portugal Cove. With the greatly increased production, and the increased number of people going to live and work on Bell island, that pier becomes all the more important. At one time last session the minister, I presume through a misunderstanding, said he was going to have that pier repaired. At a later date he said he was not going to have it repaired. As I understand it, the reason now given is that, because it is a pier for a ferry, his department is not able to do it. With the increased importance of Bell island, particularly in view of the possible war ahead, I submit that these little difficulties such as the question of whether it is or is not a ferry pier, should be overlooked and that a proper and suitable pier should be provided for the people of Bell island to use. Outside of St. John's, it is the most congested part of the whole of Newfoundland. I submit to the minister that it is a great hardship for the people of that island if they are not going to be provided with proper facilities.
The other matter that I have to thank you for, sir-as my colleague the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) has done- is the freight rates decision. But I am not so certain that there should be any great thanks for that. After all, it was a matter that was clearly laid down in the terms of union and the decision was merely implementing what should have been done without any recourse to any board or any other form of tribunal. Actually, Newfoundland was put to quite considerable expense in having to go to the various tribunals; so as a quid pro quo for what should have been done, I think it is a fair and reasonable proposition to ask for compliance with the request of the Newfoundland board of trade that proper accommodation on the newly-constructed ferry from Port aux Basques be provided for freight cars. With the dimensions of that ferry as announced by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) some time ago, it would be possible to carry twenty or thirty freight cars on it. If that accommodation was provided, not only would there be avoided a great deal of damage to goods resulting from the way they are at present carried but there would be a considerable reduction in the cost of goods going into the island. I would endorse my hon. friend's request in that connection, and I trust that the minister will bear it in mind.

There is one other matter to which I should also like to direct attention. It is paragraph 45 in the terms of confederation. The provision in subparagraph (1) is as follows:
Should the government of the province of Newfoundland institute an economic survey of the province of Newfoundland with a view to determining what resources may profitably be developed and what new industries may be established or existing industries expanded, the government of Canada will make available the services of its technical employees and agencies to assist in the work.
I do not know what the position is with regard to that particular clause in the terms of confederation, but I know that a number of outside organizations have been brought into Newfoundland, at considerable cost to the taxpayers of that province, in order to do exactly what that particular clause envisioned. I know that at the present time there are two firms engaged in making surveys. One is engaged in making a survey of power and the other is engaged in making a general economic survey. I do not know the full name of the latter firm but the short name of it is Ibec. It is an American corporation somewhat loosely associated with the Rockefellers. The other corporation is the Power Corporation of Canada which is making a survey of water powers. As I said before, I do not know whether application has been made by the province of Newfoundland for the assistance envisioned in that clause. If not, I should like to know why it was not done; and if such a request has been made, I should like to know why it was not acceded to.
There are just a couple of other Newfoundland matters to which I wish to refer. One is in connection with defence expenditures. Here I must re-echo the remarks made by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) and by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). I hope that, in allocating these expenditures, the powers-that-be will remember that for all practical purposes Newfoundland is part of Canada. It would be a great help indeed if some of that money could be funnelled into that province. During the past war there were a number of naval installations there that were of great importance in the winning of the war. I see no reason at all why those naval installations could not be brought back into active service again. At the present time they are merely lying up. They will rust out quicker than they will wear out. If I had the euphonious tones of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, I might go further into this matter. But if he and the hon. member for Royal will take it as understood that I endorse everything they said, and if the ministers opposite will do the same, I shall not trespass further with regard to that particular point.

As hon. members are aware, Newfoundland is the only province of Canada that has United States bases. As I intimated on previous occasions, we are not by any means unhappy about this fact; but I think it is about time that we again had a clear-cut statement, under the present circumstances, as to who is to take over the defence of Newfoundland in the event of war. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) visited us last summer and I believe he conferred with the United States military authorities. I feel that it would be in order to ask him to make a statement, when he has the opportunity to do so, with respect to the defence of Newfoundland.
Another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the genial Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) is the question of the Industrial Development Bank. I understand that by the charter of this bank it is impossible to obtain loans for fisheries. I think this is a matter which should be remedied. I think it is equally important that not only the fisheries of Newfoundland but the fisheries of Canada generally should be in a position to apply to the Industrial Development Bank for assistance. This brings me to the question of fish.
The hon. member who preceded me spent considerable time on wheat. Wheat is extremely important to him and to his constituents. To us fish is the most important thing in the country. Some 50 per cent of the people of Newfoundland live directly out of the fishery. Because of that fact, it can be easily realized what an important factor fish is in the economy of the country. Associated with fish is the question of being able to sell it. The bulk of our salt fish is sold to countries that have great difficulties in converting their money. I would ask the minister to be prepared to make convertibility of sterling possible at the time this new year's catch is to be sold. Last year, as a result of delayit was impossible for a considerable quantity of fish to be sold. I would also ask that serious consideration be given by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) to the idea of a guaranteed price for shore fish. Last year there was a guaranteed price for Labrador fish. I know from the people in my own area that unless something of the same nature is given for shore fish, we shall not have people going fishing this year. This is therefore an important matter and I would ask the minister to take it into consideration.
I am not in a position to endorse as strongly as I should like to the remarks made by the hon. member for St. John's West; but if the situation that he spoke about exists, then definitely a serious investigation with respect to the fisheries is required. Personally I can

The Address-Mr. Higgins hardly realize it is quite as bad as he stated; but he has made a study of it and probably is aware of what he speaks.
In that connection, last night I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) who endorsed the remarks of my colleague. I was particularly taken with a portion of the remarks of the hon. member. At page 283 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
Hitherto in this house I have refrained from speaking of things provincial or things pertaining to my riding. I did so for the very good reason that I did not want my presence here to be misunderstood.
He continued:
I believe we have been here long enough now for the people of Canada to understand, so I can now revert to form and in this speech refer to matters pertaining to my province and to my riding.
I hope that the hon. members associated with the hon. member for Trinity-Conception will also have the same feeling, because it is very important that Canada should understand the position of Newfoundland and all her troubles. I would ask the hon. members, two of whom I see opposite me this afternoon, whether they will join with the hon. member for Trinity-Conception. Let us have a united front. We might even form a maritime bloc here.
In another part of his speech the hon. member for Trinity-Conception said, as reported at page 284:
For fifteen, years in Newfoundland we had a fonn of government that we called a little dictatorship. You may call it bureaucratic, if you like.
Later on he said:
Since I have come here, particularly lately, I have found a certain amount of the bureaucratic business that we had in Newfoundland years ago.
Surely, the hon. member does not mean to imply'that this government is a little dictatorship in any way. That would be a terrible thing.

speechtext: It is a big one.

speechtext:
We all know that is the wrong name. It is not a little dictatorship; it is quite a big one by the look of hon. members opposite. I must confess it came to me as a complete surprise to hear the hon. member say this:
We now find that all requests going in are answered with one word "no," that defence comes first, and that we must economize. I would say that'there is such a thing as false economy.
He continues:
It requires no brains to say "no." You can teach a parrot to say that.
Surely he does not mean that hon. members on the other side of the house have been taught to say "no" to Liberal requests. I 
would understand it, frankly, having had the experience with requests from hon. members on this side of the house; but it is certainly new for a request by a Liberal member to be turned down. There must be something rotten in the state of Canada or in the Liberal party. What is it? At all events, it is very pleasant to hear him speaking out. I trust that other Newfoundland members will have the same spirit and will speak out in the same way. That is about all I have to say on Newfoundland affairs.
The remainder of my time I am going to devote to a few comments on outside matters.
I must confess that I was taken with the reply of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) last week to the conscription issue. As far as I am concerned it is only fair to say that he adopted a frank and manly attitude, and he is to be complimented on it. In making that statement as he did he had the advice of the Secretary of State for External Affairs iMr. Pearson). He had the advice of the various ministers of the commonwealth whom he met in London. He had the advice of General Eisenhower and General Mark Clark, both of whom he met, and he had the advice of most of the western powers. Therefore, he statement that he made would be the generally accepted statement of the government. It does not do much good to try to make any suggestions contrary to that. But before we came up to Ottawa some four of us had a meeting with the members of the Canadian Legion. My colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) and the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) and myself met with the members of the Canadian Legion and the whole matter was discussed. The matter of the brief that was submitted to the government was discussed. One remark that struck me very forcibly, as I am sure it did the other hon. members at that time, was this. We were talking with one of the officers in command of the reserves. There are three reserve regiments in Newfoundland. This commander had recently been up here. He said that in talking with his colleagues of the leserve regiments he was told by them that the Newfoundland reserve regiments were the best in Canada. The comment that he made, IVlr. Speaker, was this. It struck me so forcibly at the time. He said: "If we are the best, well, God help the rest of Canada". I am not pursuing that subject any further.
In connection with the defence committee, I must confess that the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) were very interesting, because they corroborated exactly what the leader of the opposition

(Mr. Drew) had been asking for, for some time past. Coming from a former minister for air, from an hon. member who has had such opportunities as the hon. member has had, his remarks were indeed worthy of note. I know that my adding a request would not make any difference one way or the other.
We are all supposed to be cogs in this machine of parliament. If we are cogs in that machine we should at least be able to make an intelligent survey of what goes on. Frankly, so far as I am concerned in this defence expenditure picture, I do not feel I am any better than a piece of dust in one of the cog wheels. I believe that will be the feeling of most of us. I am merely going to say we should have that defence committee.
With regard to price controls, I am entirely in accord with the stand of my leader. Yesterday I listened carefully to the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell), and I believe that his explanation was not too far away from the remarks of the leader of the opposition. With price control we must inevitably have wage control. As the leader of the C.C.F. party said, labour leaders are prepared to get around the board at any time and discuss wage control, provided that price control measures are taken. After all, we have to remember that in these days the labouring man is not the hewer of wood and the drawer of water that he used to be. He is equally well able to form judgments as any hon. member in this house. He knows the facts quite as well as we do, and if he finds it necessary to cut back his wages, then he will do so, provided always that he is getting a fair deal under price control.
With regard to the St. Lawrence seaway proposition, I must confess that I have two views on the matter. I am definitely in agreement with the need for it. As I recall it, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) said that it should be done by Canada alone, if necessary. I am entirely in accord with the idea that the seaway project should go through, with this provision, that Newfoundland and the maritime provinces generally should get some quid pro quo for it. After all, it is the ore that is coming out of Labrador that is going to go up that seaway. What are we in Newfoundland and the maritime provinces going to get for it? So far it looks only like skim milk, with the royalties and the work being provided. I do not in any way wish to condemn the possibility of the building of that 'seaway, but I do feel proper precautions should be taken whereby the province that has within its boundaries the greater portion of the ore will be reimbursed for the taking away of that ore. We must remember it is not a crop: once the ore
The Address-Mr. Higgins is extracted, it is gone. As I said, I have two views in the matter; I should like to see the seaway go through, but at the same time I cannot help feeling that in our part of the country we are being robbed to make a big iron industry in Canada and the United States.
The other matter upon which I wish to speak briefly concerns the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). With respect to him also I must confess that I was deeply impressed by the frank and free statement he made. Like some other members of the house I had the opportunity this year of being present at the United Nations, more in the capacity of an observer. While there I was extremely impressed by the minister's work. Like the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) I feel the minister played an extremely important part in the consideration of decisions of the United Nations. Certainly it was most apparent that he was highly regarded by all those present at the meetings. My own observation was that all who were associated with the minister, particularly those who served in the capacity of delegates and alternate delegates, did an excellent job for Canada in every way. In that I include members of the House of Commons.
May I add further that the permanent staff from the Department of External Affairs who served at Lake Success are extremely capable in every way. The permanent head of the delegation, Mr. R. G. Riddell, is indeed doing a good job for Canada, and Canadians may be justly proud of the work of the department in that connection. This afternoon, replying to a question by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the Secretary of State for External Affairs commented upon the crossing of the 38th parallel. As I took down his words he said that Canada has not made any representations to the secretary general as a result of the British statement. He said further that the political significance of any new move is fully appreciated, and that any decision should be collective, including those countries participating.
The English view appears definitely to be that the 38th parallel should not be crossed at the present time. I must confess that is my view, and I trust that, having secured agreement in the cabinet, the Secretary of State for External Affairs may consider making active recommendations to the secretary general that the 38th parallel be not now crossed, until [DOT] further negotiations are proceeded with.
I remember when the matter was discussed, at Lake Success in October, the minister was far from happy in having to support
326	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Higgins the decision to cross the 38th parallel. I do hope we will feel he can make the recommendation which has been suggested at this time. I feel that voting to declare communist China an aggressor was the only course that could have been pursued, and I entirely agree with him in that respect.
There is one point in that connection to which I should like to refer. The chief advocate at that time for non-crossing and for not declaring China an aggressor was Sir Bene-gal Rau. Those who read the editorial which appeared in yesterday's issue of the Ottawa Journal must have been struck by the pertinent comments of the editor. It is headed "Strange Happenings in Korea-And in India", and states in part:
When UN, on February 1, was about to proclaim Red China an aggressor, India's Sir Benegal Rau, was instructed by Prime Minister Nehru to declare:
"I feel bound to mention that my government has been informed on the highest authority that once there is a condemnatory resolution there is no hope for a peaceful settlement." Sir Benegal Rau, in sepulchral tones, closed with a warning of "disaster."
What had India heard from Red China? According to a despatch from the correspondent of Newsweek in New Delhi, India had heard nothing to warrant Sir Benegal Rau's despair. He writes:
"A state department investigation in New Delhi and elsewhere failed to disclose any basis for these dire warnings. The inquiry discovered that the Chinese, in their messages to India, had been careful not to close the door to negotiations. They had not refused, as the Indians charged, to negotiate a cease-fire while the UN resolution was pending."
And then the editorial comment continues:
During UN's debates on the U.S. resolution much was heard of Panikkar, India's ambassador to Red China; he was the man supposedly keeping Nehru -and others-informed of what Mao Tse-Tung was thinking. Interesting to note, therefore, that (according to Newsweek's New Delhi correspondent) ambassador Panikkar's daughter, Miss Devaki Panikkar, was advertised recently in an Indian newspaper as "giving the lie to western slanderers of New China." Writing on New China's glories, apparently with the ambassador's approval, she said:
"I could not help thinking how much some of our ministers would profit by a course of intense training in the Marxist-Leninist theory."
Reading this, noting its source, some may wonder. Wonder if by some chance there may have been more than appeared on the surface in the notes which, during the debates at UN, came from Mr. Nehru's ambassador at Peiping-and more than appeared on the surface in Sir Benegal Rau's efforts to stop Red China being called an aggressor.
I think that we might very well have comments from the Secretary of State for External Affairs respecting that editorial; it is one which strikes me as very important.
The last matter to which I should like to refer is the suggestion contained in some news dispatches, and particularly a United Press dispatch of yesterday headed, "Soviet Stand Towards West May Soften; Opening


of Door to Discussions Indicated." The suggestion I presume is that at the forthcoming meeting of the foreign ministers of the big powers Russia is going to try again to produce some kind of peace movement.
The main item on the agenda is the rearming of western Germany. The discussion of this item is at the insistence of Russia. I trust that our minister of external affairs will use whatever influence he has to see to it that the Russian attitude is not allowed to eat too much into the vitals of the decisions that must be made by the foreign ministers. I listened carefully to the expose of communism by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore). As hon. members know, Lenin is the interpreter of the Marxian doctrines and is quoted frequently and reverently by Stalin. It was Lenin who disposed for all time of there being any question of friendly and lasting collaboration in a statement in the following words:
We are living not only in a state, but in a system of states, and the existence of the Soviet republic side by side with imperialist states for a long time is unthinkable. One or the other must triumph in the end. And before that end comes, a series of clashes between the Soviet republic and the bourgeois states is inevitable.
In commenting on diplomatic statements, Stalin made the following statement:
Words must have no relation to actions-otherwise what kind of diplomacy is it? Words are one thing, actions another. Good words are a mask for concealment of bad deeds. Sincere diplomacy is no more possible than dry water or wooden iron.
That is the man we have to depend upon to keep the peace of the world. As I see it, there is only one way in which the peace of the world can be kept, and this is in contradistinction to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). I still believe the United Nations has a part to play in keeping the peace of the world. If there is going to be a just and lasting peace the only way we can have it is by a true parliament of man, as the United Nations has been planned. In that parliament Canada must play her part.
There is only one way in which to meet the communists of the world, and that is with a big stick. It is to have that big stick ready that we in Canada are united today. No matter on what side of the house we sit or to what party we belong, I am sure that whatever sacrifices the government deem to be necessary will have the full support of everyone. All we want is to know what we are spending the money for and to see that it is properly spent. Once we have that, you can be certain that we as representatives of the people will speak with their voice when

The Address-Mr. A. F. Macdonald
we say, "All right, go right ahead, you have the highball. Carry on down the track."
At six o'clock the house took recess.

Mr. Speaker, I trust you will permit me to add my congratulations to those already extended to the mover (Mr. McMillan) and seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, on their apt presentation. Then may I say it affords me great pleasure to be associated in this house with my friend and colleague from Edmonton West (Mr. Prudham), who is to be congratulated upon his elevation to the portfolio of mines and technical surveys. His appointment is a compliment to his constituents and to the province of Alberta.
Today, Mr. Speaker, there is a feeling of urgency in our thoughts and in our affairs. It may well be that the requirements of national security rightfully deny us the opportunity of learning full details of the plans of the government. I feel, however, that this is a time for outspoken leadership, for a clear declaration of policy and a reaffirmation of our faith in democracy. Above all it is a time for an expression of confidence in the future of our Canadian brotherhood. Our people have been given a description of the duties and sacrifices of citizenship. We need not have the slightest fear that Canadians will not respond; our most recent history is proof of that. But it is of the essence of our way of life that the people must be kept fully informed. When our people know the need they will answer the call.
Over the years great social benefits have been obtained for our people, and these must not be endangered. We must provide full opportunity for individual self-expression. We must provide safeguards for the legitimate interests of each segment of our society. We must strive to guarantee our citizens a share of the national wealth so that at least minimum requirements and necessities of life will be secured to all, for herein are contained the fundamental tenets of Liberalism and the philosophy of the Liberal party. Canada has achieved an envied position in the eyes of many of the world's peoples. It is recognized for its constructive, deliberate and fair-minded search for social justice for the disabled, the underprivileged and the aged; for its emphasis on health, welfare and education, equal opportunity for all, and a steady approach toward the goal of full employment;
and for the productive capacity of its citizens. These are fine aims, which to a very considerable extent have been realized. To go further and attain a full measure of security will be difficult, the more so under our defence economy.
We plan to spend in the next few years in this country some $5 billion on national defence. We are all agreed on this stem necessity. We will seek by every means to assure that this money will be expended in such a way as to give us the maximum possible protection. When we consider what $5 billion would do for the aged, the ill-housed and the undernourished in our country, perhaps a truer measure of the cost of this great effort can be visualized. While this vast amount must be spent on preparedness, which is basically a non-productive purpose, I submit that we must yet continue to assure our people the goods, services and rights which are theirs by virtue of their citizenship and as a return for individual effort in the national interest.
Today we should be concentrating our energies on increasing our output of vital materials. Whatever restrictions may become necessary on the output of certain types of consumer goods, or on price and wage levels, these should go hand in hand with an urgent emphasis on the production of food, clothing and in fact all the necessities of life, and the full exploitation of our immense industrial potential. We are associated with many other countries in an effort to assure national security. In our own interests, as well as in accordance with high moral principles, we have undertaken to assist underprivileged nations elsewhere in the world. Increased production will not only help improve our own living standards but will help us meet those international commitments.
Increased production alone is not enough. There must be a proper distribution of the goods we produce. With this attained our people will be prepared for the physical and spiritual part they must play in the world today. To this end the social security measures instituted by our government can make a powerful contribution. In effect our unemployment insurance provisions are a means whereby a better distribution of purchasing power is afforded wage earners between periods of gainful employment. Family allowances are also a method of redistributing the national wealth between periods of lesser and greater family responsibility. Furthermore, the recommendations of the joint committee on old age security when implemented will go a long way toward bringing about a more equal distribution, and will tend to distribute the burden on the shoulders of all. With respect to the whole field of social

The Address-Mr. A. F. Macdonald security in this country I cannot do better than quote the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as set forth by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in his submission on old age security on March 10, 1950, as they appear at page 643 of Hansard:
One of our main domestic concerns is the provision of social security for all Canadians. The funds distributed under old age pensions, family allowances, pensions to the blind, health grants and other measures have also, in addition to the direct benefit received by the direct recipients of those amounts, added a strong upward influence in maintaining levels of employment. Our social security program is, as you know, by no means complete. We still have a good way to go before provision of social security in Canada reaches the level which will satisfy . . .
In actual fact all incapacity resulting from sickness and all disability due to age are a burden upon the national wealth, irrespective of the administering authority. It would be far better if these problems were made a governmental responsibility, though not necessarily of the federal administration. A sounder, more satisfied society would result from a proper allocation of expenditure in this regard. Both locally and nationally, through municipal, provincial and federal agencies, and through the devoted efforts of many fine service and charitable organizations, we have achieved a creditable record in the field of social service. Until such time as the world situation permits us to go forward with courage and with confidence towards the bringing into being of full security for all, we must participate to the full in any other means available.
There is, however, one factor which continues to be a sore spot and that is housing. Should we not be laying ever greater emphasis upon the provision of low-cost housing, and in fact of housing generally, to meet the still well-nigh insurmountable demand for living accommodation? Until the people of this country are adequately housed, there will be bad influences which will continue to wreak havoc with family life, and the economic pressure of sustained high rentals will continue its damaging effect on the standard of living. Rent is one expense which more frequently than not bears hardest on those least able to pay. The benefit of the fairest and best thought out plaps for social security will continue to fall short of even the minimum standards for which they are designed, so long as we are short of adequate housing at a price people can pay.
I have previously made reference to the work of voluntary organizations in connection with social welfare. To my mind, it is a question as to whether we are considering TMr. Macdonald (Edmonton East).]

the objectives and methods of these organizations as fully as we might to assist them in obtaining a greater degree of effectiveness in their objectives. After all, no one will deny that the greater the degree of voluntary social betterment the easier will be the task of the official government organizations in this field, and the more in keeping with our principles of self-determination in a free society. We have, I would think, gone a considerable way along the path of recognition of the importance of voluntary aid and organization in social service, as witness our association with the national physical fitness campaign, our national health grants, vocational training and many other projects. Much of the evidence considered by the committee on old age security consisted of submissions by voluntary social service organizations interested in this field. The incidence and development of mutual aid, friendly societies and charitable trusts is an outgrowth of many centuries of the democratic way of life, particularly in the English-speaking world. For my part I would like to feel that a comprehensive study would be made with a view to determining, in the light of present-day conditions, their full significance and value in helping to bring about the kind of social organization we in this country would like to see established.
At the present time a large measure of protection is afforded groups of employees against sickness, including hospital and medical expenses, through commercial insurance bodies. One example of this is the medical benefit plan recently instituted through the efforts of organized representatives of federal civil service associations. Moreover, in addition to the many plans sponsored by industrial concerns, whether instituted by management or by management co-operating with labour, there are large numbers of mutual benefit societies which are purely associations of employees, fraternal organizations, or social groups in which the economic factor is only part of their attraction.
There are, of course, a number of societies, some of them religious, many of them participants in the community chest, which do magnificent work in social aid and welfare. Special consideration with regard to taxation for purely charitable organizations is embodied in our legislation, though I am not familiar with the provisions concerning the related voluntary service organizations.
We all know the value of the labour-management production committees set up in industry under government auspices during

the war which had as their object increasing production and the ironing out of difficulties at the source. Might they not serve as the basis for the promotion of thrift, saving and co-dependency among employee groups not otherwise taken care of by collective bargaining agreements.
In the field of co-operative saving as distinct from the object of insurance, we have the phenomenal growth of the credit union movement. The most significant development has been in the province of Quebec where the caisses populaires have had their widest growth. However, in 1948, for all Canada, there were some 850 thousand Credit Union members with assets of more than $253 million.
The history of co-operative marketing in Canada would require a volume to unfold. Perhaps the western Canadian wheat pool enterprises are among the best known of this type, and their value to the western farmer, and in the long run to the general economy, has been magnificent.
At this time when we are concerned with reducing easy credit and the building up of our financial reserves to meet an emergency, I feel we should promote the development of these and similar organizations from the point of view of encouraging saving as a bulwark against temporary insecurity and unforeseen expenditure.
This country, Mr. Speaker, has been more fortunate than many in this modern world. It is due, in a great measure, to the comprehensive policies of this government that the war and its aftermath caused as little real dislocation and hardship as has been the case. The true value of these policies during the period of consolidation and restoration from the ravages of war will be seen when we face up to the difficulties that lie ahead.
We are fortunate, too, that in this country our people continue to exhibit those pioneering qualities which have brought about our present high degree of development. This process of development, particularly in its industrial aspects, is greater, actually and comparably, than at any previous time in our history. The requirements of modern living, and of the maintenance of a high standard of living in our complex society, demand far-reaching policies and methods to permit society to function freely. We realize the problem is complicated. It is a problem which is not personal or local or even national. Our problems are international.
We are fortunate in having such a highly regarded and brilliant Canadian as our Secrete	___,,c lur External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). We of this party hold no brief
The Address-Mr. A. F. Macdonald for the socialized state with its accent on regulation-nay, regimentation. We continue to adhere to the concept of a free society where individual'initiative and energy shall have full play; where faith in the essential goodness of the individual is maintained, but where nonetheless realistic understanding of human nature, and of the influence of economic and social pressures, forces the adoption of some degree of regulation of individual activity in the general interest.
We have faith in the direction of a government which carried us successfully through the second world war and the return to a peacetime economy. It will not fail us now in preparing and concerting those measures which will give us, we trust, the wherewithal to meet the future with confidence unshaken.
Nevertheless, I would like to see the expression of our faith in our country clearly asserted, forcibly set forth at this time. Perhaps, in that war weariness that seems to possess all peace-loving nations after conflict, we fail to apprehend the need for that eloquence which can personify the spiritual values in our civilization; to realize the need for clarity of expression akin to those outpourings of the human spirit which have heretofore inspired nations to heroic effort and endurance. In such fashion in our time the genius of Winston Churchill, of Franklin Roosevelt, glowed through their exhortations to their peoples. This quality was possessed in more humble, plainer-spoken fashion by the late great leader of the Liberal party, Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, as it is by his successor, our revered Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).
There is, I maintain, no scruple, no objection or no law which denies us the right to have confidence in ourselves and in our cause, nor yet the right to express the same in forthright fashion. Let there be, however, no delay. Let us act while we speak.

In rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with all of those who have preceded me in congratulating most warmly the mover (Mr. McMillan) and the seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. All of us realize the exacting nature of the task they had before them, particularly those of us who have had the privilege of a similar honour at the opening of previous sessions of this house. These two gentlemen certainly carried out their duties in a most creditable fashion, and they deserve the words of commendation which have been addressed to them by those who have taken part in this debate.
330	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Dickey
I also wish to join with the others who have expressed the appreciation that the members of this house feel of the manner in which you, Mr. Speaker, represented this house and this parliament at the opening of the new House of Commons in London. I am sure that the members of the mother of parliaments were pleased to know that this house, this spiritual offspring of that mother of parliaments, could send a man of such obvious dignity and distinction to represent us on such an occasion.
It has been made obvious, during the course of this debate, that the members of this house recognize full well the seriousness of the situation with which this country and the nations of the western world are now faced. I find it a little bit difficult to agree with the point of view expressed by some hon. members opposite, when they have said that one of the great needs is for this house to convince the people of Canada of the great seriousness of the present situation. I cannot speak for the whole country but in Nova Scotia generally and in Halifax in particular I feel that there is a full and deep realization of the problems with which we are faced and the serious nature of those that can be foreseen in the immediate future.
The people with whom I have spoken- and I have made it a point to speak with as many as possible-have shown an awareness of what the future may hold in store and a realization that Canada and her allies must do all in their power, first of all, to avoid war and, second, to make all necessary preparations for war if war must come. Because of my belief that there is this realization by the people of Canada of the realities of the present situation, I feel that the government and this parliament can trust the instinctive good sense and the courage of the Canadian people, and that we can feel assured that if we do the things we consider necessary to maintain peace and at the same time to prepare for whatever eventualities may be before us, we can proceed with confidence that the nation will respond to whatever demands have to be made upon it.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that this country for a number of years past has been extremely fortunate. We have never experienced the real ravages of war- It is true that the price we had to pay in blood and treasure in two wars was bitter enough; but a kind Providence has always protected us from the actual onslaught of the enemy. Since the end of the second world war we have faced some difficulties, and we have had reason to complain of a number of inconveniences and troubles. But by and large, I think that our good fortune has continued. This morning I was greatly impressed by


a phrase that I read in a pamphlet put out by the Department of Agriculture. In discussing the question of the food situation in the world this pamphlet said that the per capita food supplies in most countries are still below the 1935-39 level. What a picture, Mr. Speaker, that draws for us in Canada, a country which has for some years past, I understand, enjoyed a per capita consumption of all the essential foodstuffs, and many that are not essential, that has been the highest in our history. I would direct attention to the fact that this is per capita consumption, not per capita supply. In spite of increases in prices which have been significant and serious enough, and have been one of our major causes for complaint over the last two or three years, the vast majority of Canadians have been in a position to increase their consumption of such a fundamental thing as food while other countries have been facing, an actual deficit situation with regard to supplies. I think also of the significance of the phrase "most countries." That does not just include the countries we have always regarded as being in a normal deficit position. It includes the majority if not all of the countries of western Europe which is the very cradle and birthplace of our civilization. It is not unreasonable to suppose that this good fortune to which we have become accustomed might have created a sense of complacency in the Canadian people; and this is probably the basis for the statements which have been made by hon. members opposite, and to which I referred. I may be wrong, but I am personally convinced that such is not the case. I am sure that no feeling of complacency exists among the Canadian people. In my humble estimation Canadian public opinion is alive to the dangers of the present situation, and the Canadian people are prepared for forthright action and leadership. Leadership by the government and by men in public life will find a ready and loyal response from a vast majority of all the Canadian people.
Our most important and essential activity at the present time is our struggle to keep the peace. This struggle to keep the peace is after all, by every possible means of comparison, our best and first line of defence. If the outbreak of a new war, which appears to loom more imminent day by day upon the horizon, can be prevented, the saving te humanity will be incalculable. We might just ask ourselves: can any price be too high to pay to ward off this terrible catastrophe of human suffering, waste and futility? I think the answer is that no price can be too high which leaves our honour unsullied and maintains our essential freedoms. The scene of this battle for peace is the difficult and complicated field of international relations.

During the recess of the special session I was one of the members who had the privilege of having a glimpse of this all-important side of Canadian policy during the fifth session of the general assembly of the United Nations. I hope that on another occasion it may be possible and appropriate for me to deal at greater length with the experiences which we all shared there. However, what I want to say tonight is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is making at a cost of prodigious labour and at the expense of tremendous energy a truly magnificent contribution to the strengthening of our vital first line of defence.
I have been particularly pleased to note, Mr. Speaker, the almost universal approval and esteem in which the Secretary of State for External Affairs is held by the people of this country. This is a second instance to which we can point in which public opinion in Canada is at the present time particularly sound and firm. However, I should like to point out to both his friends and his enemies, if he has any enemies, that behind the Secretary of State for External Affairs in all his actions and in the stands which he has so courageously taken in the name of his country is the solid backing of his colleagues in the cabinet, and particularly our great Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).
The activity of second importance which we have before us in these days is that of our preparations for collective defence. Defence is such an essential matter that it is almost impossible to describe it as secondary to anything else. It is perhaps a paradox of our age that the only thing we can possibly regard as more important than the building up of the armies and armaments of ourselves and our allies is our equally strong and tenacious efforts to ensure that these arms and armaments will never be put to their intended use. However that may be, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has outlined to the house the government's program calling for expenditures of $1,600 million this year as part of a $5 billion three-year program. I am sure that the announcement of this program in the house gave us all a very solemn thrill.
In his criticism of the defence program the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) saw fit to point out that under the rules and procedures of the house we are limited to the commitment by the government of $1,600 million. He appeared to set quite some store by that. Then, shortly afterwards, he turned around and admitted that it was perhaps very wise for the Minister of National Defence to disclose the whole program. It was particularly wise because I am quite sure that if he had not done so it would have been seized 80709-221
The Address-Mr. Dickey upon as another excuse for claiming that no information has been given on defence matters. I believe that this kind of criticism is, Mr. Speaker, a very clear indication to the house and to the country of a complete inability to discover any valid basis for criticism, and of satisfaction with the small kind of carping criticism that I have outlined.
My judgment of the temper of the Canadian people is that they are not inclined to question the amount or the size of our defence program; but they are-and I hope they will always be-very much inclined to question how the money is to be spent, and to make sure that it is spent in the best and the most economical way. With this in mind I am sure that a very vast majority of the people of Canada are greatly satisfied to know that by and large the members of the opposition have indicated their support not only for the broad basis, the broad lines of defence policy as outlined by the minister, but also for most of the details. This is a very reassuring situation from several points of view, as my colleagues will agree. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, there will be other opportunities for discussing very fully the details of the defence program and spending. I do not propose to make any more extended remarks on that subject this evening.
Last evening the debate in the house turned to the consideration largely of economic and financial policies. This, under present circumstances, is of course inseparably linked with our problems of defence and of meeting the costs of defence. I am sure that all hon. members and the public generally were very appreciative of the frank and able speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I think this house was expecting a clear statement from the minister on the steps being taken by the government to curb inflation, and, particularly in view of the widespread public interest in the question of controls, of the government's view on that very important matter. It is true that the cost of living is only a symptom of inflation; but it is a very painful symptom, one which touches every person in Canada and bears particularly heavily upon those least able to bear the burden. The C.C.F. subamendment to the address in reply deals with one of the suggested means-and in my view a very partial means-of meeting one of the problems relating to inflation. As I understood him, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) in his remarks last night supported, on behalf of his group, the C.C.F. subamendment. In fact, I understood him to say affirmatively that the C.C.F. subamendment was included in the amendment and that it was really only stating in words what was actually there in any event.

The Address-Mr. Dickey
To me this conjures up a most interesting picture, an inviting picture I may say, that is quite apart from the obvious public interest in a statement of that kind. The picture I see is that of a student of political science a few years hence looking up the records of parliament-Hansard for the twentieth parliament-and reading the debates of the sessions from 1945 to 1949. He would read there the resounding speeches which one can almost hear still echoing in this hall, speeches of the then leader of the opposition, speeches of the then hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, the present member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell); speeches of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming); speeches of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe); speeches of the then member for Broadview, of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson), of the hon. member who then represented the constituency of Rosedale- to name only a few of them.
What was the burden of all those resounding speeches? It was the absolute and imperative necessity to get rid of each and every control that had been placed upon the Canadian economy during the war.

Then our student of political science turns to the records of the twenty-first parliament, and reading the debates of the session of 1951 he comes across the speech delivered last night by the leader of the opposition, and speeches of ten or twelve other hon. members opposite. What does he conclude from those? I am sure the only conclusion to which he could come would be that of confusion thrice confounded. I am quite sure there are very few members in the house, either on this side or in the ranks of the official opposition, who are quite sure whether or not the official opposition is supporting the C.C.F. subamendment because it is' for a system of over-all controls, including wage controls, or whether they- are supporting it because it is a system of selective controls specifically excluding wage controls.

wage controls must be part of the program; and there is some suggestion of that kind in the speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins), and those of some others.

Perhaps we could deal with that particular bit of ice-skating at some other time.
I turn now to some other aspects of the impact of our defence program on the Canadian economy. I should like to dwell with particular emphasis upon the necessity of the greatest possible attention being given to a decentralization of the new industry it will be found necessary to set up. I should like to place certain considerations before the government, and I do so most sincerely indeed.
I hope as the situation develops it will be found possible to take action along lines currently being suggested. It is quite obvious Canada is going to undertake a great industrial effort, and I think that the Canadian people are most anxious that that industrial effort be carried forward with the greatest possible effect and to the greatest possible extent.
This is the second time in a generation that Canada has embarked upon a program of this kind. We are going to try to do our bit, as one of the great arsenals of democracy; and the extreme ends of the country, east and west, are clamouring for an opportunity to play their proper part in this great effort. I wish to join with other voices raised in the house and in the other place-and may I say this is a regular broadside at the government, and we should not forget there is another place-outlining to the government the necessity for making some long-range plans for decentralization.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley), the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and a number of others speaking in the debate have brought this subject to the attention of the house. I venture to mention it again this evening because this matter has been the subject of very serious study and discussion by a number of groups of members for some months past. It is our intention to bring our views before the government as strongly as possible.
Hon. members will recall the situation that faced us in 1939. With very little warning

we were involved in an all-out war with a very serious opponent; and for some considerable time we, as part of the commonwealth, fought almost alone. It was therefore a situation where speed was of the essence in our industrial mobilization. Because of the economic difficulties which immediately preceded the outbreak of war, there was a pool of labour available in the industrialized portions of the country, and that pool of labour was a skilled pool. I think there were very good reasons why those advantages had to be taken into consideration and used. The result was a serious concentration of industrial development in the central part of the country. Perhaps it is unnecessary for me to say that I was not a member of this house at the time, but I well remember the representations that were made repeatedly to the government by maritime and other members early in the war and throughout the war pointing out the situation which was growing up and which eventually became a fait accompli.
The situation is now quite different. Canada is enjoying a very buoyant economy, a situation which is described as full employment. To say that there is full employment reminds me a little of something said in "Animal Farm". It was discovered that there was a saying among animals that all were created equal, but some of the animals were more equal than others. Canada is enjoying full employment, but some parts of Canada are enjoying fuller employment than others.
One place where there is a ready pool of labour is in the maritimes and eastern Canada. There exists there a pool of workmen possessing great ability and great adaptability ready for recruitment. They are not all by any means unemployed; many of them are employed but in positions which do not give full scope to their abilities. A great deal could be accomplished by a reallocation of labour. We have there great resources in the way of steel, coal and other raw materials. We have also a great advantage in our geographic position. We have immediate access to tidewater twelve months in the year, and that is of great advantage in the present situation. I submit to the government that these are compelling reasons for giving consideration to these factors when industrial expansion is being carried out.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has warned the house and the country that a danger of direct attack exists. That was not so in the last war except for some danger from shelling from the sea. The situation in Canada today indicates that consideration should be given to the dispersal
The Address-Mr. Dickey of industry in order to avoid the possibility of our industry being completely hampered by one or a series of aerial raids.
Another consideration which should not be lost sight of is the advantages which accrue to the economy of an area in which industrial; mobilization takes place. I think we all recognize the importance of ensuring as much as possible the equal development of all sections of the country. It is impossible for one section of the country to enjoy great prosperity if other sections are not in a similarly favoured position. The advantages to the economy are of two kinds. First is the direct advantage of the employment created in an area by war production. Second is the much more important advantage derived from the availability of the plants which have been created for defence needs when those needs have passed. This availability was the basis of the great peacetime expansion of industry which occurred in central Canada during the five post-war years. This has been the experience in the past and I am sure that in the future when the need for defence industries will have passed as we hope it will, the stage will be set for a further industrial expansion for peacetime purposes. I submit that it would be of inestimable value to Canada if a large proportion of. that peacetime expansion were to take place in the maritimes and the western parts of Canada.
I should like to attempt to drive home my points, and to do this I should like to cite one example which I think will show exactly what I have been trying to point out. During the last war an aircraft repair plant was constructed at Eastern Passage with government assistance. That plant was operated during the war by the Clarke-Ruse Aircraft Company. After its usefulness for that purpose had passed, the plant became vacant and remained so for some time. Through the co-operation of the provincial and federal governments the Fairey Aviation Company of England acquired the plant about two and a half years ago and this establishment is now a thriving industry which is literally bursting at the seams. It is making an indispensable contribution to the economy of that particular section of Nova Scotia. In addition this plant is carrying out repair and conversion work on naval aircraft with an efficiency and economy that I know is a source of considerable satisfaction to the officers of the Department of National Defence.
That is an example of what has occurred over and over again in connection with defence plants that were constructed in central Canada during the war. I appeal to the.

The Address-Division
Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and to the government generally to consider the case, which has been made by other speakers much better than I can present it, and to give every possible assistance in the process of the decentralization of our defence industry.

Mr. Speaker, when I took part in the debate on the second or third day of the present session, I said little about the defence of our country because at that time I did not wish to attempt to criticize the government's policy without having their program in front of me so that I could give it careful consideration. As a result, we now feel that we are quite capable of assessing the whole program and of deciding for ourselves whether or not it is adequate. We feel that in some measure at least we can give support to what the government has proposed as its program for meeting the situation

that confronts us today. As a matter of fact, I suppose with a great many of the things they propose we can find ourselves in complete agreement.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if it would be possible to have more order in the chamber.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. It was hard enough for me to hear myself, let alone to have others hear. I of course realize that hon. members think they are not missing much, and I do not blame them, at this stage of the game. But at the same time I have something to say that may prove to be of interest to one or two people anyway, and they are entitled to hear. There is freedom of speech in our country. I think there is something that is equally important, and that is freedom to be heard. All too often that freedom is overlooked in this house.
The government's program calls for the spending of $5 billion for defence in the next three years. We know that Canada will have to spend a great deal of money if it is to get ready to meet the dangers that we see about us. We know that if we are to prepare ourselves adequately it will cost us a great deal of money. But it seems to me that altogether too much emphasis has been placed upon the amount we are going to spend and far too little on the details of the ways in which we are going to spend the money.
I cannot help feeling that a good many who have spoken in this debate have been of the opinion that just because we were going to spend $5 billion in three years, which means about $1,600 million a year, that was all it was going to take. But anyone with a lick of sense knows that is not so. It is not how much money we spend that is going to count. In the end, it will be the wisdom with which that money has been spent that will tell the story. We think that anything less than the amount that has been proposed to be spent in the next three years would certainly not be enough. When I say that altogether too much emphasis has been placed on telling the world how much we are going to spend in our budget for defence purposes in the next three years, I do not mean to imply that we expect the government to talk too much about the details of their plans. But what I do suggest, Mr. Speaker, is that those of us who are in this house, and observant and intelligent people throughout the country who are able to see what the government is doing, should judge for themselves whether or not the action that is supposed to go along with $5 billion of spending is wise action. Quite frankly I cannot begin to see that the government is moving along a line of action that
The Address-Mr. Low will prepare Canada, and ensure that we can make an optimum effort-perhaps I had better say the maximum effort of which we are capable-to defend ourselves.
I quite agree, too, Mr. Speaker, that in our defensive effort the main emphasis ought to be placed upon air power. I think the hon. member for Quebc South (Mr. Power) made a notable contribution to the debate. I read it with very keen interest, because I felt that the hon. member knew the situation and knew what he was talking about. I certainly feel in agreement with him that our main effort ought to be in the realm of the air. Certainly the Canadian people seem to me peculiarly adapted to aerial activity, aerial warfare. I think, too, that Canada should emphasize the strengthening of her navy. That is something with which we agree.
I agree that a country as large as ours and as blessed with resources, natural resources, but with a very small manpower such as we have, must measure its contribution more in terms of material than manpower. When I say "measure its contribution more in terms of material than manpower," I mean by that the contribution which we make to the defence of Europe or of any other country outside Canada. I hope that I can make that particularly clear because it is important to the case which I want to make.
Certainly, if war should come upon us again-I am one of those in the house who have expressed the hope that it will not come again-if it should come we do not want to make the same mistake that was made in world war II, when we practically bled our country white of manpower and put ourselves into an almost impossible position with respect to reinforcements when reinforcements were needed. We ought to be careful not to bite off more than we can chew in any effort that we do have to make to fulfil our commitments under the Atlantic pact.
As I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) last night describe the steps that his government expects to take to cushion our economy against further inflation, I thought that he was very forthright and perfectly sound in so far as his description of those steps related to the orthodox system that he persists in following. I could agree with him perfectly if I could make myself believe that he simply has to stay within the old accepted orthodox financial policies; but, Mr. Speaker, I have to criticize the Minister of Finance and the government very severely for their stubborn refusal to make use of subsidies for what I consider today are two most urgent purposes. One of these purposes is to encourage production of those things of which we have

The Address-Mr. Low an insufficient supply in our country, and the lack of which may make us weaker in our effort to prepare.
The second of those purposes is of course to mitigate to some extent the terrible effects of the very high cost of living. The government could have helped immeasurably, through a wise use of subsidies over these past two or three years.
I quite agree with what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said last night in that respect, and I do not need to repeat it because he said exactly what I think. I also feel very critical of the failure of the finance minister to use the Bank of Canada as it should have been used over these years. Ever since 1935 the government has refused stubbornly to make use of the Bank of Canada to regulate the supply of money in this country at a level of balance with the goods and services that were there to be purchased, and as a result of the failure we have gone on to a condition of inflation that simply need not be.
When the Minister of Finance jumped on the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell) I thought that he did not quite know what the hon. member for Greenwood had said. I am in agreement with the hon. member for Greenwood- when he says that the Bank of Canada could have exercised an overall supervision of banking in this country to the extent that we would not have today such a terrible inflationary condition.

know what the Bank of Canada had been doing either.
