That is perfectly correct. When the Minister of Finance says that the Bank of Canada cannot do that of course he is perfectly right unless and until this government supplies it with a policy under which it will operate. What we are asking the government to do is to supply it with that policy. It seems to me that one of the most important things we have to do if we are to prevent a recurrence of this sort of inflationary condition in the years to come, and established as a result of an all-out effort for defence, is to put the banking system of this country on a 100 per cent reserve basis.
I do not see any other way by which we can ensure that the country will not be flooded with inflation time and time again.
I do not know but I do not believe that the hon. member for Greenwood believes that.
I am not suggesting for one moment that he is joining me in making that proposal, but I will say this: that coupled with a program of that type it would become necessary for the Bank of Canada to get a money provision to supply the government with whatever


money it requires at any time to augment the supply that is in the country at the present time for making available to the people goods and services that are there for them to buy. When that is done, and only when it is done, can we ever hope to cope with the inflationary dangers that arise out of lack of regulation of the money supply such as we have today.
We feel that the present financial policy of the government, a policy which has caused disaster time after time down through history, has brought us to the brink of complete break-down more times than one can speak about in the short time that he has in this debate. It seems surprising to me that we continue to believe or hope that that same system will bring us through other dangers such as those we have passed through, without causing a break-down. It is just impossible for it to do so, and we cannot hope for an all:out effort, we cannot hope particularly for an effort of preparedness that will spread the sacrifices over the population of Canada in anything like equality until we do have a sound and sane approach to the policy of finance.
I said there are many things with which we can agree in the government's program, but we do deplore the fact that the government has failed to take appropriate steps to ensure a greater measure of equality of sacrifice and service in their program of preparedness.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke in the debate he expressed his conviction that we were living in a time of emergency, a time of grave danger. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), speaking in Montreal just a day or two ago before a delegation of the Canadian Lumbermen's Association meeting at the Mount Royal hotel, is reported in these words in the Montreal Gazette of today:
The behaviour of the Soviet union and its allies and satellites in the last six months has shown that they are more prepared than we had previously estimated to take risks which may lead to a third world war. For that reason there is no escaping the conclusion that we must arm ourselves and quickly, and assist our allies to arm. We must accept that necessity.
I emphasize the words, "that we must arm ourselves, and quickly". I accept that; I agree. But I am asking the government this question: Where is their program that arms us so quickly? That is the whole, the nub, of the situation now. Where is that program?
I have not seen any, and they certainly have not given evidence, so far as they have divulged their program to the house and country, that they have a program that will make it possible for us to arm quickly. I assume in the absence of it that there is no such program.

I must say I have not been able to find very much urgency in the government's proposals thus far. In the debate to date it seems to me we have spoken as if most, if not all, the causes of world chaos stem from Russia. Consequently there seems to be an attitude that all we have to do is to build a wall against Russia.
Let me emphasize once more, as I did when I spoke before in the debate, that there are deeper things to be concerned about- deeper things. What we have to be concerned about is this: What is it that made a bolshevik Russia; what is it that made Russian imperialism, and made those things possible? They are results, not causes.
It seems to me we must be aware of the forces that have caused the growth of a bolshevik Russia, and made her strong and a menace now to the world. World chaos today stems from attempts in practically all the democracies to build upon decadent systems and wrong principles. What we have to do is to set out to change those wrong principles to right ones, to do away with decadent systems -financial, economic and otherwise-and try to build our democracies on sound and solid rock.
If we do that we can abolish the things that have caused Russian imperialism and the spread of the evil doctrine of communism throughout practically all the countries of the world. True, we have to build some sort of wall now, and it is very urgent that we get that wall built. At the same time however we should be concentrating considerable attention upon the weaknesses in our own way of doing things that have given rise to these evils which now menace us.
I have listened to the speeches and examined them all but, as I said, I have not seen any evidence in the government's program that would ensure equality of sacrifice in the things we have to do. In all the debate I have gained the impression that there has been altogether too much pussyfooting on the matter of manpower. I do not think there is any question about it at all. There has been a lot of skating around, and a lot of shying away and soft pedalling the business of manpower. I think about the only man in the house who spoke true to his convictions, and boldly, was the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). He let us know exactly where he stood, and made certain proposals to which I think it would be wise for the government to pay heed.
Let me deal for a moment with this question of manpower. There is no question about the fact that if we are going to make the maximum effort in our own defence, and if we are going to fulfil our obligations in
The Address-Mr. Low any regional pacts to which we have given our allegiance, then we have got to make the wisest possible use of the manpower within Canada. As I have already said, I am convinced that our greatest contribution to any external effort, wherever that may be, will be in materials, not masses of manpower. Because our country, big as it is and wealthy as it is, has a small population. Let us lay that down first and foremost, and definitely.
But on the other hand I do not think the government can possibly begin to make preparations it ought to make without carrying on immediately a national registration. We are calling for a national registration just as fast as the government can get at it. We feel that not only will Canada need to know where its available manpower is, what kind of manpower is available and of what type, but it will also need to have a well trained citizenry ready to take the offensive in any danger that threatens our country. And the only way we can have that is to have compulsory training of our Canadian people for home defence. We are calling for the compulsory military training of our Canadian people in readiness for anything that menaces our shores or our land. At the same time that we are calling for national registration and compulsory service for training our citizenry so that they can be ready and so that they will know how to do things, we think every community in Canada ought to have a well-trained group, small though it may be, with sufficient equipment so that they may know how to use it, and not only how to use it but be prepared to use it in case things do happen making it necessary.
I know isolated parts of our country where it would be the simplest thing in the world for an enemy to drop airborne troops. Who says they may not attempt to do such a thing? Certainly we are not so isolated that that could not happen, if Russia decided it would be wise to get hold of certain areas within this vast country, from which to launch, let us say, rockets with warheads composed of atomic machinery of some sort. How far would we be able to take care of a situation like that under present circumstances? It would not take much of an airborne force to cut communications and transportation in certain vital parts of our country and thus render us impotent. There is only one way to deal with a situation like that, and that is1 to set out now to build up a reserve force in Canada which will be indeed a reserve force, something of which we can be proud and under which we can feel some security. [DOT]
We have got to begin-it should have been done long ago-to train leadership, those

The Address-Mr. Low who can train and take the lead in every community in Canada in putting our people through the type of training they require. Where is that program now? Has the government something like that? If so, why has it not been presented? I suggest it is because they are afraid to present it.
We feel that while we are attempting to prepare ourselves adequately with respect to the proper distribution of manpower and the preparation of a well-trained citizenry in home defence we ought to be trying to organize our financial and economic preparedness so that they will guarantee that in everything we have to do there will be equality of sacrifice for our people. I do not think it is fair for the government to expect to go on through this emergency as they went on through world war II, and again further back through world war I, expecting the people of this country to make an all-out effort to build equipment and provide materials for an all-out war, to supply an army that will be a credit to the country and guarantee that the forces of right will be victorious; to expect them to make supreme sacrifices, in many cases to give limbs and eyes and other parts of their bodies in this great effort; to pay for the war in that way and then when the whole thing is over to come back and have to pay for it again two or three times. That is not right or just, but that is what has happened. That has been the effect of our financial approach to this business of war and defence.
There must be a change. How many of our boys who went over in world war I and world war II came back and said, "We thought we had paid for the war with our *efforts." But then they were taxed to the very last cent they had and kicked out. As one of my colleagues has said, they were allowed to languish without decent jobs or .any form of security during the thirties. That was the result because we did not have the gumption to lay down a financial and economic system that would make it unnecessary for those fellows to pay through the nose and in *every other way and then come back and pay for it again with dollars and cents.
We also call for an all-out organization that will make it possible for us to defend ourselves and to help other countries that require our materials to defend themselves. The strongest possible Canada should be the slogan. Canada should be able to do her utmost. We have thought, along with many other speakers, that in the industrial effort that is to be made due consideration must be given to the claims of western Canada and the maritime provinces for industrialization. I listened last night to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) and I must say


that he made a very good speech and offered some practical and forthright suggestions.
One of the things that he asked me to do was to try to get the province of Alberta to make available to the Pacific coast part of the gas being found in that province so that the people down there may also be able to make an effort. I appreciate very much the suggestion and request he made, but if 1 were to ask the hon. member for Comox-Alberni to send to Alberta about two-thirds of the logs that he cuts so that they might be manufactured into finished lumber, I wonder what attitude he would take? I do not think he would look on it with very much interest.

I should like to point out that the province of Alberta set up a commission to study the whole matter of reserves of gas. That commission gave the most earnest consideration for quite a long time to this matter. If there is one thing we try to do out there it is this: When we set up a royal commission and that commission makes its report we do not like to be like so many other governments I could name and not do anything about it. We feel that if we have confidence in the personnel of a commission when it is set up we ought to be ready to accept their ' advice when they make their report.
That is exactly what we are trying to do in Alberta. For the benefit of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni I should like to quote from the report of the board as follows:
The board finds that Alberta's present established gas reserves are approximately equal to the amount of gas the board estimates is necessary to ensure the present and future requirements of the province and accordingly recommends that these reserves should be further increased before the export of gas is approved.
There may be differences of opinion about the extent of the gas reserves, but that is the considered opinion of the board experts who studied the whole thing, and who heard all the evidence that anybody wanted to present. When that report was presented the Alberta government decided in its wisdom that the best thing to do was not to give any permits for the export of gas from the province until further reserves were made available.
I understand that Mr. Manning's government has laid down a policy of inducements to private enterprise to come into the province, to make an all-out effort to find further gas reserves and to see that those are made available as quickly as possible. I say to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that if by this autumn those gas reserves have been augmented sufficiently I feel satisfied that

the province of Alberta will then give its consent to the export of gas to those areas that require it for an all-out defence effort.
At the time the Alberta government made this announcement with respect to the gas reserves Mr. Manning announced that if in the meantime, that is between now and September next, the government of Canada feels that it is necessary to have gas in order to make an all-out effort for our defence, all they have to do is to ask and they will get it. That statement was made by Mr. Manning just a short time ago.
There is one other thing I should like to mention. Just after the close of the last war the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), speaking in this house, criticized the Alberta government for not taking advantage of all the things it could have taken advantage of at the time to industrialize or increase its industrialization. If I am misquoting the right hon. minister I want to be corrected.

That is what the minister said. I do not agree with his criticism. I did not at the time and I think I said so. But badly as we need industrialization to balance our economy in Alberta, certainly it would be unwise and foolish in the extreme for us to send out of our province the materials and power we need to industrialize. So we say let us take some of the industrial effort out there. I have already suggested that we make an effort to set up steel manufacturing right at our own coal beds, and I think it can be done. I believe it would be in the interests of this country to do so. Certainly we will need the gas and other things that come from oil production if we are to have industrialization.
Because I have not seen any evidence, in what the government has proposed to us thus far, that the government has in mind an all-out effort, because I think we agree with practically every principle laid down in the Progressive Conservative amendment but we believe it does not go far enough, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw):
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following as clause 4:
4. To ensure that a complete program of preparedness including compulsory training in the reserve forces for home defence be executed with the greatest possible degree of equality of sacrifice and service.
Just to make absolutely clear what we are calling for, let me take a moment or two to review. Our amendment calls for a financial organization which will provide a guarantee
The Address-Mr. Kickham to all the Canadian people that there will be equality of sacrifice, as far as that can be achieved, in anything we have to do to defend our country and to assist other countries to defend themselves. Our amendment would call for an industrial organization for all-out defence production which would build Canada into the strongest possible country. Our amendment calls for a well-trained citizenry ready and equipped to defend Canada. We feel that only by following the terms of that amendment can Canada hope to make the effort that will devolve upon her in the next few months.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I wish first to join in the expressions of sympathy tendered to the families of the late J. L. Douglas and J. E. Matthews. Of Mr. Douglas I can say, as the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacNaught) said, that he ever extended a kind, sympathetic and helpful hand. In my close personal association with him I found him always putting forth ardent efforts for the welfare of his constituency and the province he loved.
I should like to make a few comments on the railway strike of last year. We in our province were severely affected by that strike, because of our insular position. The terms of union guaranteed us unbroken transport communication. The federal government placed in the hands of the Canadian National management the operation of the ferry boats connecting Prince Edward Island with the mainland. When the railway strike was called the two ferries operating were tied up at the docks. After frantic negotiation carried on by Premier Jones, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), the spokesman for the railway union, Mr. Hall, finally condescended to permit one ferry to operate until the strikers went back to work. It seems to me that we have arrived at a critical stage in the economic life of our province when the leaders of labour unions can practically abrogate the terms of confederation which we took as a sacred trust to assure our province continuous transport communication with the mainland. This matter deserves the most serious consideration by the government. Measures must be taken now to see that a similar situation does not occur in future. It should be borne in mind that the people of Canada are the owners of the Canadian National. They vested power in the government to operate the railway and the government in turn passed on the duty of management to the officials of the railway. The goods carried by our railroads result from the industrial efforts and endeavours of the people; therefore when

The Address

Mr. Kickham the employees of the people refused to carry these goods it was a case of the tail wagging the dog.
Coming from a province where the people are largely producers of agricultural products, fish and pulpwood, naturally I have some comments to offer on our industries. Potatoes, our principal farm cash crop, have been terribly disappointing to the growers for the past two seasons because of depressed market conditions in the United States. The real cause of these market conditions, I believe, is the action of the United States government in assuring minimum price support for their growers. That, of course, is their right, but it has had a depressing effect upon market values in Canada.
The continuous increase in freight rates has also had an adverse effect upon our potato industry. At times the railway receives more for a bag of potatoes than does the grower. At the present market price per bag the railway is splitting with the grower on a fifty-fifty basis. If the board of transport commissioners would grant the maritime potato industry preferential freight tariffs it would be of great assistance in eliminating distress. Assistance similar to that given the western grain growers in marketing feed grain in eastern Canada and the maritimes, which is also of great benefit to the farmers of eastern Canada, should be implemented to assist our potato industry.
In our fishing industry, last season the lobster catch was very good. We had strong markets with satisfactory prices, especially for the fresh market catch. On the other hand the prices for hake and cod were disappointingly low, only two to two and a half cents per pound for the green fish. Efforts are now being made by the departments of fisheries, both federal and provincial, to assist the industry in the operation of draggers of a lesser tonnage than now receive assistance. Other matters of concern to the fishermen in the field of packing and processing the by-products are also under consideration. In this industry there is great need for improvements which, when put into effect, will be of the greatest assistance.
I should like to support the request of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) for the decentralization of war industry whenever that can be effected. Premier Frost of Ontario has referred to the problems created by the centralization of war industries in already crowded cities and municipalities, in connection with housing, and so on. In the maritimes, where some war industries could be established, the workers already have their homes and other facilities for home life, thus eliminating the housing problems which must be faced in concentrated

areas. The distribution of war industries over wider areas is also an important defence factor.
I notice a trend of thought permeating some members' speeches to the effect that Canada has an obligation to assist east Asian countries, technically and economically. While this may be without question a worthy objective during a time when the gross national production of Canada has climbed to over $17 billion in 1950, indicating a boom condition in most of Canada, no such economic condition exists in the maritimes. Caution should be exercised against too great exuberance, because these may turn out to be but temporary economic conditions. In this respect we should remind ourselves of the old adage that charity begins at home. This provokes the thought that the maritime provinces could avail themselves of surplus federal capital to great advantage in many fields. For example, it would be an advantage to the farmers in our province, the producers of poultry, eggs, dairy and beef cattle, hogs, potatoes and fish. Western feed wheat now costs $4.25 per hundredweight. If the government, through some medium such as subsidies, laid down this low-grade wheat and other grains in the maritimes at $2 per hundredweight, it would stimulate the production of these products. This would ultimately lead to lower costs for the consumers, and would enable the western farmers to market low-grade wheat and other grains here in Canada. There is also an urgent need for financial assistance to the fishing industry.
There is another group of citizens who are continually asking for assistance, namely our war veterans of the past two wars. They are requesting pensions, veterans' allowances and widows' allowances. The Department of Veterans Affairs apparently has not now the authority to satisfy many claims that appear to be justified. In this connection, I am pleased1 to note that amending legislation will be introduced at this session, as indicated in the speech from the throne, for the purpose of reaching veterans who are now beyond the scope of this legislation. All in all, there are numerous fields in Canada in which capital investment would be rewarding.
Many people who have practised prudence and frugality all their lives, and who contributed through direct and indirect taxes to the treasury of the dominion government, about which they have not complained, are now protesting over the arbitrary and exacting decisions of the income tax branch. I do not think they would take too kindly to having their money given to Asian countries, either as risk capital or in other ways.
In conclusion, I should like to urge upon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) the

The Address-Mr. Shaw
necessity of providing winter boat service between the port of Georgetown, in Prince Edward Island, and Pictou, Nova Scotia, after the two ferry boats servicing the route between Wood island and Caribou are forced to discontinue because of ice conditions in Northumberland strait. Premier Jones has pointed out that the ferry boat Prince Edward Island is idle during the winter months, and would be suitable to continue this service. Since the distance is only thirty-eight miles the boat could make one round trip per day, thus enabling our shippers and others to carry on regular business relations.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when concluding his remarks in this house on February 1, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) moved an amendment. That amendment read as follows:
That the following words be added to the address:
"We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed
(1)	to give this nation leadership in the face of the present grave danger; and
(2)	to bring into being forces necessary to enable Canada to defend itself and discharge its international obligations; and
(3)	to take effective measures to combat inflation and the rapidly rising cost of living.
As my leader indicated a few moments ago, we found nothing to complain about so far as that amendment was concerned, except that in our opinion it did not go far enough. Accordingly, he moved an amendment to the amendment as clause 4:
To ensure that a complete program of preparedness including compulsory training in the reserve forces for home defence be executed with the greatest possible degree of equality of sacrifice and service.
Mr. Speaker, in seconding that amendment I agree wholeheartedly with all of the observations made by my leader. In essence we are asking the members of this house to endorse the Canadian Legion's program for total preparedness. With certain very notable exceptions this debate, Mr. Speaker, has been characterized by brevity, and I shall make an effort to keep my remarks particularly brief.
Before continuing, I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. McMillan) and seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As indicated by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) some days ago, one's first speech in this house is a rather trying experience. It is more trying when the speakers are new to the house, particularly when they have come to parliament via the by-election route. In my opinion the two hon. members acquitted themselves in a commendable fashion.
The discussion during this debate thus far has, quite naturally and quite properly, revolved around the extremely critical international situation, and the acute danger which confronts all free democracies including our own. His Excellency's address referred specifically to the deterioration in the international situation, and to the menace in the Far East which reinforces the mounting evidence that communist imperialism is determined to dominate the world by force or by fear of force. Quite apart, Mr. Speaker, from anything that was said in His Excellency's address, and quite apart from anything which has transpired since mid-June, there has certainly been ample evidence to convince anyone who is open to conviction that communist imperialism has set as its ultimate objective the complete domination of the free, democratic world of which we are a part.
As indicated yesterday by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), all one has to do is go back to the communist manifesto itself to learn to one's own satisfaction what that goal is. He indicated that in the manifesto itself it is stated for all to see that their belief and conviction is that communism-call it by any particular name you like-and capitalism, so-called, cannot live side by side in the same world. Subsequent actions and declarations on the part of communist leaders have certainly provided clear evidence that, right from the date of that communist manifesto, there has been no departure whatsoever from that avowed purpose.
I often say to myself that communism has become the greater menace because communists everywhere know exactly what they want. They are united in that purpose of complete domination and enslavement of the free world. Unfortunately there were all too many who, down through the years, could not or would not comprehend the significance of what has taken place in certain European countries. We think of Hungary, Roumania, Czechoslovakia and so on. In all parts of the free world, including our own country, there were people who gave evidence of simply closing their eyes to what had taken place. Tragically there have been altogether too many who have not seen, and have not been willing to see, what has taken place right in our own country.
It is not too long ago that some of us who kept repeatedly referring to the growth ol the communist party in this country and the dangers of communism were told that we were just looking for bogeys in clothes cupboards. If the truth were known today, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the members

The Address-Mr. Shaw of this house and the people of this country would be shocked at the numerical strength, if 1 may put it that way, of the communists within our own nation. I realize fully that it is probably not possible to advise this house and the country of the counterespionage activities which have been under way. I realize that in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police we have an agency which, limited by its strength, has been doing excellent work in this field. But if there are in the neighbourhood of 20,000 or 22,000 card-carrying communists, and if there are 8 to 10 sympathizers for each of that number, surely we know what could happen overnight within this nation should Russia decide to move forward in the next step toward world conquest. Realizing that danger, and realizing how ill prepared we are today to meet that menace within our own country, does it not become absolutely essential that within Canada we establish among our people a type of organization by means of which our people shall be trained and equipped to meet not only what may come flying over the ocean but what can occur right within our own country? It is that consideration more than anything else which governs my thinking and which motivates me when I refer to the necessity of placing our Canadians in a position where they will know what to do and how to do it, and will be equipped to do it, if a situation of that kind develops. Let us not pass off too lightly that word "if." I have great confidence not only in the willingness but in the eagerness of our people to be prepared, to be trained and to be equipped to meet whatever may happen in our own country.
As was stated by my leader, Mr. Speaker, we regret many of the things that have taken place in the past. For example, we regret that it is only at this rather late date that we talk of the Colombo plan and of rendering technical assistance to the unfortunate peoples of certain other lands. It is most regrettable that that has not been our avowed policy down through the past many years. Is it any wonder that in certain parts of the world constantly hungry people have been swayed, have had their affections alienated and have turned their eyes away from countries like our own which were capable of doing so much to help them in their affliction? I think of our trade policies and our failure to understand that there cannot be peace with the "haves" and the "have nots" endeavouring to live side by side. I deplore certain of our policies; but being a realist I hope I am not unmindful of the great urgency that exists in connection with the necessity of building up a strong defence wall around our own country. We hope it will not be soon; in fact, we hope

that it will never occur; but let us govern our actions with the thought foremost in our minds that it may be soon when a ruthless and unprincipled enemy may be hammering at that defence wall. Let us also bear firmly in mind the fact that, as I said earlier, it will not be purely a matter of the enemy being without that wall; there will be an enemy within-alert, ready and trained-to unlock the gates of that wall; and the password is "sabotage." Do not mistake the truth of that statement. As I said a moment ago, we have a big job to do quite apart from defence. We have a job to do in winning back the affections of many of those people elsewhere in the world who have turned away from us.
This amendment of ours, Mr. Speaker, called for that training and that preparedness which is so essential; but it also referred to that question of the greatest possible degree of equality of service and sacrifice. When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke with respect to the manpower question a great many thoughts went through my mind, as they always do when manpower in relation to war, or to defence, is mentioned. My mind goes back to some of the things mentioned by my leader tonight. Some may assume that in the past we have enjoyed the highest possible degree of service and of sacrifice, but surely that was not so. Thousands of our boys joined the various branches of the armed services and went out of Canada. Many of them left their wives and children. They passed the whole of the war in distant battlefields, or in the skies# over the battlefields, or on the sea. They came back, and, as indicated by my leader, they were faced with the unhappy and extremely deplorable situation of the colossal debt. The thought constantly went through their minds what the acting minister of finance had said in 1939, namely, that as far as it is humanly possible we shall pay for the war as it is fought. They came back greatly disillusioned. And when I hear this talk today of a lack of housing for those veterans; when I learn today of the continuing grievances with respect to various items of legislation affecting veterans; when I realize that there were families in the country who expanded their holdings very materially during the war as a consequence of all members of the family being at home while others in many instances were obliged to see every male member of the family depart, in my opinion there was not even a remote approach to the question of equality of sacrifice.
Referring also to this question, I should like to think, Mr. Speaker, that, when the Prime Minister spoke earlier in this debate

and asserted with respect to our manpower question that sentiment would not be a deciding factor, there would be no mobilization of manpower simply for the sake of mobilization, when he -took exception to the doctrinaire anti-conscriptionist, when he said that sentiment, race, and creed were not valid factors, when he said that the decision would be made purely on its merits, I agreed with him; but I had to conclude that he had not gone far enough. I thought there was an air of optimism about him and about what he said that to me at least could not be justified in the presence of the obvious facts. I would have appreciated hearing the Prime Minister saying something like this when he spoke that day. This is somewhat similar to what I should like to have heard him say: While not a pessimist or an alarmist, I am a realist. Communist imperialism constitutes a deadly threat to Canada. This country is a logical military target. Moreover, it is vulnerable to attack. Then he could have gone on and said: The effective defence of this great democracy involves several essentials: first, rapid and maximum production of required defence materials; second, the establishment of strong defences where such defences -are deemed necessary within our country; third, the immediate implementation of a program of compulsory military training, without exemption, in reserve forces of this country; fourth, there would be an immediate inventory, call it registration, if you like, of our human resources within this country; fifth, the adoption of a financial policy to obviate much of the need for oppressive debt and subsequent interest charges such as those which were built up during world war II; sixth, effective action to deal realistically with the cost of living problem; and seventh, and final, immediate action to prohibit the accumulation of huge profits resulting from war.
May I repeat, Mr. Speaker, had I heard the Prime Minister of Canada make an assertion of that kind I could have gone to my room and rested more comfortably than I did the night of the day on which I heard him speak.
Early in the last war, on September 12, 1939, to be exact, the acting minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, speaking in -this house, said this, as reported at page 140 of Hansard -he was referring to the method of financing:
All this is not to say that a small and carefully regulated amount of credit expansion may not be desirable in the early stages of the war in order to assist the increase of production and employment. It must be small and carefully controlled because its effects which may not appear immediately are cumulative and otherwise might get out of hand.
The Address-Mr. Shaw
In the same speech he said:
However, as soon as the expansion of employment and production gets well under way and certainly before it approaches its limits, further expansion of the supply of money and credit must be stopped if the danger of progressive inflation is to be avoided. With an economy at full production and employment, the only result of expanding money and credit is to raise prices without increasing production.
It is with these fundamental considerations in mind that we have decided upon our policy of war finance. Because we believe it is the part of wisdom, we shall follow as far as may be practicable a pay-as-you-go policy.
Not only initially but throughout all the years of world war II the government of Canada persisted in its policy of heavy borrowings from the chartered banks. This was a significant feature of government financing. I am told-I have not confirmed the figure myself-that they borrowed over $3 billion from the chartered banks, and spent it throughout those years of the war and continued this quite contrarily to the position laid down by the minister of finance himself during the war. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but they went out during the war loan campaigns and instead of telling the people, as they should have told them, that they were trying to meet and correct a condition of inflation resulting from too much money in circulation, they told the people that the only way you could have ships and shells and guns and tanks would be for them to subscribe their savings. But the very nature of the campaign resulted in hundreds of thousands of those people going to the chartered banks and borrowing newly created credits, thus adding millions upon millions, hundreds of millions more to an already highly inflated condition resulting from the government's persistent policy of borrowing from the chartered banks all during the war.
In 1939 the bonded debentures and treasury bills of Canada amounted to $3,385,722,462. Then ten years later, according to the Canada Year Book, it had jumped from that figure to $15,585,036,580. The actual interest-bearing debt was greater than that. What effect was had upon the interest? The annual interest charges in 1939 were $129,077,904. Now, in spite of a lowering of interest rates on borrowings by the government in the latter years of the war, the interest jumped from the figure I have given to $442,059,153.

speechtext: And no "sense".

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And no "sense", as our leader has said. You can take that in its broadest sense. During the war, taking into account the deaths and our wounded, generally categorized as casualties, we had about 100,000.

The Address-Mr. Shaw We blew-into kingdom come, as some say- approximately $20 billion worth of production. Substantially as a consequence of the pursuance of that inflationary policy of borrowing heavily from the chartered banks, the boys came back and, with us, face a debt of $16 billion, as compared with the former three and a half billion, with interest charges of $442 million per year as compared with $129 million at the time the war broke out.
If there were any justification whatsoever for a situation of that kind I would be reasonable enough to accept it. But surely I cannot accept that, especially when we may never be advised by the government exactly what part of this debt was held by the chartered banks, nor have we been given a break-down to show what percentage of the bonds sold went back to the chartered banks through default on the part of purchasers.
In 1939 the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, then prime minister, said, as reported at page 23 of Hansard for September 8:
I come to profiteering. I believe I have already stated in this house that I know of nothing in the world more contemptible than that any man should seek to profit from the sacrifices which others are making . . . Unfortunately human nature has its weak and its bad sides, as well as its strong and good sides. Sometimes it is very difficult to cope effectively with the underworld and its methods. I care not who the individual may be, how respectable in his own eyes or in the eyes of others he may appear, or what position he may hold; if in this crisis he seeks to profiteer he belongs to the underworld and should be treated as one of those who menace all that is sacred in human relations.
When one comes to the definition of a word one finds a wide divergence of opinion. One person may think of profiteering quite differently from the way I would think of it. But when I stop to think of persons who entered the field of war production, there come to my mind some people who did not have a dollar to start with. Through a policy of cost-plus'- and as a member of the war expenditures committee of that time I am one who knows there was lots of "plus"-coupled with a rapidly accelerated rate of depreciation on buildings and machinery, men who had virtually nothing when the war started came out of the war as wealthy men. I well recall the time that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking in the house on September 12, 1939, referred to the five per cent ceiling on war contracts which had been put into effect under the defence purchases act. While I was not in the house at the time, having come here a few months later, I recall clearly having read in Hansard at that time where the minister spoke specifically about the fact that there was not one tender, as long as that five per cent proviso existed in the provisions for defence purchasing.

The proviso for limited profits was eliminated in, as I say, those, in many respects, devilish cost-plus contracts. I am not saying that a government can go into a period of war production now, when there are so many component parts which have to be imported, and a certain number of uncontrollable factors, and say at the commencement of a contract, "This is to be the end price." But, in my opinion, looking back as a member of the war expenditures committee I think there was a great deal of laxness that should never be allowed to prevail again. There should be far stricter supervision where cost-plus contracts are in operation.
I for one, so long as I am here, shall insist upon that. I think, too, we had better watch this question of rapidly accelerated depreciation, because a lot of people in this country are fed up with what occurred at that time.
Mr. Speaker, I believe I have spoken beyond my allotted time, but I do not think anyone else would desire particularly to start just before eleven o'clock. I am sure anyone following me would favour my going on for a few moments more.

Dealing with that section of our subamendment which refers to compulsory training in the reserve forces, I cannot but refer to a letter which came to me from one of my constituents only yesterday. I have received the telegrams from the various branches of the Canadian Legion and have made no decision purely on the basis of those telegrams. I participated in a good many meetings of one kind or another during the past several months, and I know what people have told me. I know what I have been told ' on the street. This man's letter reflects in an admirable fashion the feeling prevailing in the constituency of Red Deer. This man is not the type who is likely to go off the deep end. This man is a solid citizen, a good type of man from my home community. He is a substantial farmer and under date of February 8, he wrote:
I feel that all good men and true who have the honour and security of this' great dominion of Canada at heart can do no less than endorse the Canadian Legion's "Operation Preparedness."
Therefore, sir, I hope you will not cease to press upon the government at every opportunity the need for action upon the terms laid down therein and particularly, as a first step, the urgent need for national registration and compulsory training in the reserve forces.
The taxpayer knows the price will be high, but not so high as the cost of unpreparedness. I know that I speak for a great number of your constituents in this matter and while not desirous in any way to emulate the system of our good neighbours to the south, I feel nothing but disgust for the soothing reassurances emanating from the government. Time is short and this is not the time for political expediency.

The Address-Mr. Shaw

In conclusion, may I say that all of us hope and trust that there will be no third world war, but all of us know that possibly for the next quarter of a century we shall have to feel somewhat as though we are at war. Earlier in my remarks I said that I like to be branded as a realist. Secondly, such training would avoid panic, which is one of the things
that could be really bad. It would develop confidence in our people. Speaking personally, I think it would be good for one's physique-not that I have much of a physique even though I spent more than a year in that type of training.
